newObjects.Name: UGC 9037
newObjects.Historical:
z = .020 --> Hubble distance ~300 Mly.

2022 paper by Bisaria+: "Non-circular flows in HIghMass galaxies in a test of the late accretion hypothesis." (2022MNRAS.509..100B)
We posit that UGC 9037 harbours a weak inner bar that is shuttling gas toward the galaxy centre, consistent with the high inner H I and CO surface density measured in this system and suggesting an upcoming episode of star formation (Section 4.1).
-----

2014 paper by Hallenbeck+: "HIghMass–High H I mass, H I-rich galaxies at z ~ 0 high-resolution VLA imaging of UGC 9037 and UGC 12506" (2014AJ....148...69H)
We present resolved H I observations of two galaxies, UGC 9037 and UGC 12506, members of a rare subset of galaxies detected by the ALFALFA extragalactic H I survey characterized by high H I mass and high gas fraction for their stellar masses. Both of these galaxies have M* > 10^10 M_Sun and M_H I > M*, as well as typical star formation rates for their stellar masses. How can such galaxies have avoided consuming their massive gas reservoirs?

From gas kinematics, stability, star formation, and dark matter distributions of the two galaxies, we infer two radically different histories. UGC 9037 has high central H I surface density. Its gas at most radii appears to be marginally unstable with non-circular flows across the disk. These properties are consistent with UGC 9037 having recently acquired its gas and that it will soon undergo major star formation.

2019 by Sil'chenko+: "The gas kinematics, excitation, and chemistry, in connection with star formation, in lenticular galaxies" (2019ApJS..244....6S)
UGC 9519. This is a dwarf lenticular galaxy elongated in PA = 75°. However, in the frame of the ATLAS-3D survey an outer H I ring was found by Serra et al. (2012), well beyond the optical borders of the galaxy, which is elongated in the north–south direction. newObjects.Name: Sh 2-116
newObjects.Historical:
Stewart Sharpless included this planetary in his 1959 catalogue of HII regions (Sh 2-116) and the 1991 paper "A comparative study of morphology and velocity field of the emission nebulae S153, S207, S211, S212, and A71". He concluded this is an HII region, based on the lack of (or very low) OIII emission (http://cdsads.u-strasbg.fr/full/1991PASP..103..843P). But more recent papers in the literature consider Abell 71 as a PN.

I contacted David Frew in September 2007 and he replied, "I think the interpretation of this nebula as a HII region comes from Pismis, Hasse & Quintero (1991), but they erred on this one.  It is certainly an evolved elliptical PN, with evidence of an ISM interaction.

It is more distant than I assumed before (cf. Frew, Parker & Russeil 2006), but is still reasonably nearby (D = 1.4 kpc, from my revised H-alpha surface brightness - radius relation).  It is reddened (A_v = 2.3 mag) and would be a much easier object visually if it was unobscured. 

The central star may be unresolved binary based on the available optical and near IR photometry (again my own unpublished work)."

18" (11/26/03): about two dozen stars in a 3.5' group at 160x.  Five brighter mag 10-12 stars form a small "Y" asterism in the center with the northern star a nice mag 11/12 double at 10".  The brightest cluster member is a mag 10.5 star at the east end of the "Y".  Most of the other stars are richly sprinkled around this "Y" and are mag 13.5 and fainter.  A faint stream of stars extends out of the core towards the north.  Berkeley 4 lies 15' NNE.

17.5" (8/18/93): about 25 stars in a 6' diameter.  Includes three mag 12 stars in an equilateral triangle.  The northern vertex is a nice double star (mag 11/12 at 10" in PA 66°), 2' SE of this double is the brightest star in the cluster-a reddish mag 10-11 star.  About 15 mag 13.5-14.5 stars are peppered over the triangle.  Mag 7.2 SAO 11343 lies 9' NW.

visualUpdates.Name: Berkeley 4
visualUpdates.Visual Description: 18" (11/26/03): this is an interesting cluster of ~10 stars in a central 2' clump including mag 9.5 SAO 11367 with two fairly close mag 10.5 companions at 11" and 30".  Another mag 11.5 star is 45" NE.  This clump is partially enclosed by a semi-circle of mostly mag 13-14 stars running from west to east around the south side which may also be part of the cluster.  Finally, there is a distinctive "V" shaped asterism of 8 mag 10.5-12 stars with the vertex facing east about 5' following the main group.  King 16 lies 16' SSW.

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 246
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
48" (10/23/14): At 488x with an NPB filter the view of the Skull Nebula was breathtaking and all the structure in a detailed photograph was visible.  The thin brighter rim varied in brightness, thickness and scalloped structure along its entire length.

The rim is brightest along a 60° arc on the western side, bulging inward just north of center, creating a small darker indentation in the rim due west of the prominent central star. Moving counterclockwise around the rim, a small brighter, elongated patch is at the northwest edge, close to a mag 11.5 star just outside the planetary.  The rim is relatively weak along the north side, but two brighter (detached) patches are along the northeast side.  An irregular, elongated luminous patch spreads inward here.  This glow is fairly prominent just northeast of center, on line with the central star and the second interior mag 12 star (southwest of center). A second luminous patch is midway from the central star to the north rim.  The rim is weakest overall along a 90° arc on the eastern side, near a mag 13.5 star, which is embedded just within the planetary. Two more luminous patches are visible at the south rim, with the westernmost glow both larger and brighter.

The interior is relatively dark, though glows weakly with subtle variations, creating pockets of darkness - one is northeast of the central star - and mild enhancements.  A small diaphanous glow is just south of the mag 12 star on the southwest side.  More extensive milky nebulosity extends inward from the southern rim, though the most prominent interior glow is the split nebulosity mentioned earlier on the northwest side.

33" (9/15/07): gorgeous annular planetary viewed at 200x.  The thin brighter rim was striking and varied in brightness and thickness around the periphery.  The rim is brightest along the western or WNW edge and weakest on the east side.  The interior was darker but irregular in surface brightness.

18" (10/13/07): 175x gave an excellent view using the NPB filter and the thin, bright irregular rim (only dimming on the east side) and darker center was quite striking.

18" (8/23/03): I took a quick look at 160x from Chew's Ridge with a thin waning crescent low in the ENE.  Without a filter I don't remember the brighter rim being so crisply defined and the annularity so clear.  The superimposed stars gave the planetary a transparent, 3-dimensional feel as if I was seeing inside the object.  

17.5" (1/8/00): at 100x, appears as a moderately bright, 3.5' irregular glow with a darker center and encompassing four stars including the 12th magnitude central star.  Excellent contrast gain using an OIII filter, which sharpens up the edge of the roundish annulus and enhances the irregular surface brightness.  The halo is brightest along a 270° arc running from SW to NE and is clearly weakest at the east edge of the halo.  A mag 11.5 star is embedded at the NW edge of the halo 2.0' from center.  The irregular central hole is much darker but faintly luminous.  A mag 12 star is also superimposed southwest of the central star and a 4th star is just inside the eastern boundary.  The central star forms a thin right triangle with the other two brighter stars.  At 220x, the western 90° outer arc is brightest and there appears to be a knot embedded at the NE edge of the halo.

17.5" (9/19/87): fairly bright, large, 4' diameter, annular.  Four stars are involved including the central star.  This planetary has an irregular surface brightness with subtle structure. 

13.1" (many dates from 11/13/82 to  8/24/84): fairly bright with filter, clearly annular, sharper edges.  NGC 255 lies 15' SSE. 

8" (11/5/83): fairly faint, large, four stars involved.  No annularity noted.

16x80mm finder (8/24/84): faintly visible in the finder.

80mm finder (10/13/07): visible unfiltered at 25x.  Nice contrast gain using the NPB filter and the planetary also appears to increase in size.

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 300
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
25" (10/21/17 - OzSky): at 187x; bright, extremely large, irregular, elongated roughly 5:3 WNW-ESE, at least 15'x9'.  Contains a large, brighter core region with a mag 11.5 star at the ENE edge of the core.  A mag 9.6 star is in the halo (along a faint spiral arm), 2.6' SW of center and a mag 10.6 star is superimposed in the outer halo, 5.3' SE of center. Spiral structure was surprisingly subtle. A low contrast, broad inner arm extends W from the N side of the core, curls S on the W side and spreads out. A more obvious inner arm emerges from the S side of the core and sweeps E and N, though the root of the arm is not defined.

The arm passes through a relatively bright and large HII patch/OB association, ~25" diameter, situated 3.9' E of center and loses contrast further N. This giant HII complex is catalogued as #65 in a 1966 paper by Sersic and #137 in a 1988 study by Deharveng et al, "H II regions in NGC 300."  A mag 11.5 star is 2.3' further NE in the outer halo of the galaxy. I didn't have time to examine the galaxy at higher power to search for additional H II knots.

13.1" (9/22/84): fairly large oval 3:2 WNW-ESE, very diffuse appearance, bright stellar nucleus.  There is a hint of structure although the galaxy has a low surface brightness and was viewed at a low elevation (13° at most) from my latitude of +38.5°.  This nearby galaxy is located at a distance of 6 million light years in the Sculptor group, and may be physically paired with NGC 55.

15x50mm IS binoculars: (11/18/06): visible in binoculars as a relatively large, very low surface brightness hazy region, roughly 15' in size.  A star is superimposed on the SW side.

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 330
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
25" (10/17/17 - OzSky): at 397x; extremely bright, fairly large, elongated NW-SE, ~1.5' diameter, high surface brightness cluster.  Easily over 20 stars were resolved in the central region and more than three dozen including outliers around the periphery.  NGC 330 is situated in a rich, glowing section (Hodge Association 40) of the SMC just 20' SW of NGC 346, the top HII region in the SMC.

18" (7/6/02 - Magellan Observatory, Australia): this is one of the brightest SMC clusters and a fascinating object at 228x.  It appears as a bright, extremely rich knot of stars, just 1' to 1.5' diameter, which was only partially resolved.  Streaming out from the dense core were numerous mag 12 and fainter stars, some arranged in a curving chain off the following side of the core.  The bright outliers seemed scattered about to at least 5' (Hodge Association 40).  NGC 330 is situated 20' SW of the remarkable HII region NGC 346 within a rich star field!

10x30mm IS binoculars (11/4/12 - Coromandel Peninsula, New Zealand): visible as a very small, but non-stellar knot.

visualUpdates.Name: IC 59
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
18" (12/22/11): best view was unfiltered at 108x.  Appears as a faint, large, irregular glow, roughly 8'x5'. Elongated E-W and extends to a group of a half-dozen stars at the NE end.  This group of stars is also possibly involved with the haze.  There is a slightly brighter patch on the south side.  Located 25' N of Gamma Cas.

18" (7/15/07): this large emission & reflection nebula is just 20' N of Gamma Cas (Navi). It has a low even surface brightness and appears as a large oval-shaped hazy region ~6'x4', that is elongated ~N-S.  Fainter of pair with IC 63 located 25' SE.

17.5" (11/1/86): located 20' N of Gamma Cassiopeia.  This emission nebula is larger than IC 63 but has a lower surface brightness.  Easy with averted vision and appears large, elongated ~N-S, with a fairly even surface brightness.  IC 63 lies 20' SE.

13.1" (11/5/83): very faint, fairly large, very diffuse, visible with averted only.  Forms a pair with IC 63.

visualUpdates.Name: Stock 3
visualUpdates.Visual Description: 18" (11/26/03): small group of only 6 mag 13 stars in a small 1.5' wedge shape.  These stars are detached in the field but are very unimpressive visually.

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 456
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
18" (7/6/02 - Magellan Observatory, Australia): this is the first in an unusual chain of three nebulous clusters with NGC 460 and NGC 465 within 10'.  The best view of the entire group was at 171x using an UHC filter.  At 220x, NGC 456 is the largest in the trio, appearing as a roundish 3' glow with a very small elongated knot embedded in the SE end (SMC-N83A).  A few stars are superimposed (Hodge Association 61) on the glow including the mag 13.5 O2-3 type star AzV 476 near the center. HD 7583, a mag 10.2 SMC supergiant (A0-type), is 3’ SSW.  NGC 460 lies 4' ESE.

10x30mm IS binoculars (7/6/02): visible as a faint glow..

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 522
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
18" (12/3/05): NGC 522 is an attractive, edge-on slash with a slightly brighter core. It extends 1.2' x 0.2' in a SW-NE orientation and fades at the tips. It appears uniformly narrow in width (does not bulge in the center). NGC 525 lies 17' S within the NGC 524 group.  A couple of faint members, IC 101 and IC 102, lie 10' SW and 8' SW.

IC 101 is a faint hazy spot, irregularly round, ~20"-25" diameter.  A mag 14.5 star lies 1' S. IC 102 is extremely faint, very small, 15" diameter, no details.  This marginal object was just glimpsed as drifted through the field.

17.5" (10/17/87): faint, pretty edge-on steak SSW-NNE, weak concentration.  Located 27' N of NGC 524 in a group. 

13.1" (8/24/84): very faint, edge-on streak SSW-NNE.

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 628
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
48" (10/22/11): beautiful face-on spiral with long, graceful arms wrapping around an intense 1' core that increases towards the center, but there is no sharp nucleus.  At first glance at 375x there appeared to be four arms, but with a more careful look there are two main arms that each wrap more than 360° around the core as well as a couple of side branches.  Each arm is studded with a number of non-stellar HII regions that highlight the arms.  In addition, a number of stars are superimposed, both in the inner region (two faint stars are within 25" of the center) and around the edge of the halo, which extends to 7'-8' diameter.

The more prominent arm "southern" arm is very regular - emerging from the core on the south side and wrapping counterclockwise around the core to the north, unwinding gradually as it curves to the east and then pulls away from the central region more suddenly on the south side.  This arm is very patchy and delineated by a large number of HII knots with the two most prominent ones near the outer southern end.  The "northern" arm begins to emerge from north of the core, tightly wraps counterclockwise around the core, passing near or through a few superimposed stars on the south side of the core, unwinding more as it stretches again to the north.  The arm structure is a bit more complex on the north side due to side branches and the embedded HII knots are more scattered.

The HII regions were viewed more carefully at 610x.  The following identifications are from Paul Hodge's 1976 "HII regions in NGC 628" (ApJ, 205, 728), which lists over 700 HII knots.  The brightest is #627, near the end of the outer southern arm 2.7' SSW of center. It appeared fairly bright, fairly small, round, ~20" diameter.  Moving clockwise along this arm towards the core, the next prominent knot is #598 situated 2.2' SSE of center.  It was slightly fainter than #627, round, 15" diameter.  Next in line is #552, a faint round knot of 10" situated 1.8' SE of center.  East of the core by 1.5' is #406, a very faint, round 10" knot situated 36" S of a superimposed mag 14.5 star.  Just 30" W of this star and 1.2' NE of center is #292, a fairly faint, very small knot, ~8" diameter.  Continuing inward along this arm, the next knot is #196, a very faint hazy spot 1.3' N of center.  Finally, less than 1' NW of center is another very faint patch with multiple Hodge numbers #260-268.

There were no notable knots on the inner southern portion of the northern arm, but a noticeable clump of knots is on the NW portion of this arm.  First was #167/168, a faint 10" knot 1.6' NW of center.  Continuing outward 2.0' NNW of center is a faint, elongated patch, ~25" diameter, consisting of #91-95 and #49 at the north end of the glow.  I didn't search the outer region of the halo for additional HII knots, except noted #330, a 10" knot situated between two mag 12-13 stars at the eastern edge of halo, 3.9' from center.

24" (8/7/13): viewed type IIP SN 2013ej, discovered on July 25th, 92" E and 135" S of center.  It appeared bright at mag 12.5.

17.5" (2/2/02): viewed type Ic SN 2002ap, discovered just 3 days earlier on Jan 29th. The supernova was easily visible as a mag 12.5 "star", situated 4.6' W and 1.5' S of center.  This very energetic event is considered a hypernova, resulting from an extreme core-collapse scenario.

17.5" (8/31/86): bright, large, round, very bright core.  A spiral arm is attached at the east side of core winding towards the west along the south side.  A dark gap is visible between the arm and the main central portion.  Several stars are superimposed in the halo.

13.1" (8/24/84): very prominent, fairly small bright core surrounded by a very large, diffuse glow.

8" (many dates from 10/4/80 to 8/24/84): very small bright core surrounded by a large faint halo. Fairly even surface brightness.

16x80mm finder (8/24/84): visible in the finder.

visualUpdates.Name: IC 166
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
18" (12/22/11): easily picked up at 175x though at this power appeared as a faint, fairly small, roundish glow.  At 285x ~10-12 mag 14-15.5 stars were resolved with a couple at the edge of visibility over a mottled background.  Roughly 3.5' diameter.  A brighter mag 12.5 star is at the west edge.

17.5" (8/5/97): I identified the position at 100x using a Guide Star Catalogue chart, although only a couple of stars are plotted.  It appears as a very faint circular glow with a couple of faint stars superimposed.  Located 7' E of a wide pair of mag 9/11 stars [at 38" separation].  It does not resemble a cluster in appearance and I would have otherwise thought this was a Milky Way patch. At 220x, the glow is ~4' in diameter and there is a sprinkling of ~10 very faint stars, mostly mag 14.5-15.5 with one mag 13 star.  The glow has an irregular surface brightness with a mottled appearance and the periphery is not well defined.

visualUpdates.Name: Sh 2-190
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
NVD at 1x (1/20/25, 2/25/25): The "Heart" Nebula (IC 1805) and "Soul" or "Baby" Nebula (IC 1848) form a prominent night-vision pair handheld at 1x. IC 1805 is the brighter and slightly larger of the pair. It appeared slightly elongated or irregular in outline.  NGC 896 is a small, bright knot at the NW end or just detached.

14.5" (12/4/24): NVD at 24x; fantastic showpiece at 24x, though the entire nebula doesn't fit in the field.  The NGC 696/IC 1795 Superbubble is extremely bright and has the highest surface brightness of the complex. The main patch is bisected by a prominent dust lane that curves gently from N to S. The brighter W section, which forms a rough half-circle, is itself brightest at the W end (this is part seen by Herschel).  An irregular dust patch is to its east.  The section E of the lane is irregular and tattered on its E side.  Extending to the north are several knots and patches of various sizes and shapes that seem affected by dust.

The main loop forming the "Heart" outline is really too detailed to described, but here are some features I noted:  A sharply curving filament oriented ~E-W defines the N edge. The NE side consists of a curving arc oriented N-S. A straight outer wing shoots NE from this end of the nebula.

A very large "U" shape portion of the heart begins at the indentation of the "Heart" and extends south, before curving back W and finally NW.  The SEern border pretty thin. A fairly high surface brightness, irregular patch is along the SE side of the nebula.  The SW rim also has a high surface brightness with an irregular structure. Nebulosity seems to flow inwards and pools in a patch near the center.  A detached patch (about 5' diameter) is just off the SW side.

The interior of the Heart is filled with faint, wispy nebulosity, but a very bright 10' irregular patch is north of center in the interior.  It was detailed with filamentary structure and involved the central part of the cluster Cr 26 = Mel 15.

14.5" (10/6/23, Albany): NVD at 24x; I took a look at the Heart and Soul Nebulae (just the third night using the device) in the backyard -- and once again I was amazed the amount of structure visible in the very bright conditions. I was pleased to find both nebulae individually nearly fit in a single field of view (over 1.2°).  I started at NGC 896, at the NW end of the "Heart Nebula" (IC 1805), which was quite prominent and show low contrast dust lane(s).  Extending south of the east end of NGC 896 (this is IC 1795), a huge fairly thin strip extended south for over a degree, then curved on its south end towards the east.  It could easily be traced bending north and stretching 1° north, forming a huge loop.  The stream of nebulosity then bent back west towards NGC 896, but didn't quite connect.  Just before bending west, a thin finger of nebulosity branches off to the NE!

NVD at 1x (11/30/21):  The Heart and Soul Nebula (IC 1805 and IC 1848) are bright, prominent patches only 4° to 5° from the Double Cluster.

visualUpdates.Name: Sh 2-199
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
NVD at 1x (1/20/25, 2/25/25): The "Heart" Nebula (IC 1805) and "Soul" or "Baby" Nebula (IC 1848) form a prominent night-vision pair handheld at 1x.  IC 2848 is the slightly fainter of the pair, but is still quite bright and large. It extended 2:1 E-W,  ~1.7° x 0.85°.

NVD at 1x (11/30/21):  The Heart and Soul Nebula (IC 1805 and IC 1848) are bright, prominent patches only 4° to 5° from the Double Cluster.

visualUpdates.Name: IC 348
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
5.5" (1/14/26): at 54x; the cluster appears as a loose collection of 10 stars that are partially involved in a nebulous glow (reflection nebula) on the N side. Barnard 4 is a very large, starless region to the south of the cluster.

8" (1/14/26): at 71x; about a dozen stars easily resolved in the loose cluster IC 348.  The region surrounding mag 8.5 HD 281159 is clearly involved in an irregular, nebulous glow that is elongated roughly to the northwest.

24" (1/14/26): at 200x; bright, scattered cluster centered 8' SSE of Omicron (38) Per). It includes about 15 stars down to mag 14.5 in a 6' circle. In the central region is mag 8.5 HD 281159, which has wide mag 10.5 and mag 11.5 companions (STF 439). Several of the outer stars in the western half form a semi-circle.  STF 437, an equal mag 9.8/10.0 pair at 11" separation, is outside the group to the SW.

The cluster is enmeshed in a strong, irregular nebula  (vdB 19), which is brightest in an elongated NW-SE region centered on HD 281159.  Barnard 4 is a large, striking region devoid of stars due to dust to the S of IC 351!
 
17.5" (12/16/95): IC 348 is located 5' to 10' S of mag 3.8 Omicron Per (38 Per).  This unusual object consists of a scattered group of stars with associated nebulosity (vdB 19), and it's situated near a large dark cloud that's virtually devoid of stars.

The cluster consists of 15 stars of varying magnitudes in a 6' group.  The brightest (and most massive) star in the cluster is mag 8.5 B5-type HD 281159, which has two nearby companions.  The group is clearly encased in a fairly bright reflection nebula, ~3' diameter.  The star at the SW end of the cluster is STF 437, a nice evenly matched pair of mag 9.8/10 stars at 11).  The immediate 50' low power field to the S is strangely devoid of almost all stars! (this is DN Barnard 3 and 4).  Omicron also has a halo but this appears to be scattered light.

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 1499
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
17.5" (1/16/02): Despite its reputation as a challenging target, this was an easy, fascinating object at 64x with a H-beta filter. The California Nebula is HUGE and extended a full two eyepiece fields even using a 31 Nagler for a total length of over 2.5 degrees and with a varying width of 15'-30', extended WNW-ESE.  The E-W border is well-defined with a filter, particularly in the general vicinity of Xi Persei (middle of three naked-eye stars in the leg of Perseus collinear with the Pleiades) on the southern border and a long straight stretch on the northern edge.  Along the northern edge, there is some filamentary, wispy structure similar to the view of the Veil nebula in a small scope!

The nebulosity is weaker and more disorganized, though, close to the preceding and following ends. The nebula tapers towards the eastern end where there are some additional brighter streaks and dark intrusions near a group of stars.  Portions of the central region are clearly fainter with no evident structure.  At the west end the structure is also chaotic with an irregular mix of weak nebulosity and darker voids.  There is much to view here even at 64x, and I spent 30 minutes scanning the entire length for structure. 

17.5" (10/28/89): the California Nebula requires very low power and visibility is best using an H-beta filter.  At 82x appears very large, faint, very elongated, irregular low surface brightness with darker lanes and some wispy structure along the edges.  The most well-defined section of the border is near a mag 8.5 star bordering the southern edge.  Located roughly 30' N of mag 4.0 Xi Persei.

13.1" (1/18/85): definite contrast gain with H-beta filter as only the section NW of Xi was definite using a Daystar 300 filter (siimlar to UHC), but the H-beta shows the full extent easily.

13x80mm (1/13/07): excellent view in my 80mm finder using a 24mm Panoptic and an H-beta filter as a huge, elongated bar of fairly high contrast stretching across the field.  The glow is generally brightest in the broad middle section between Xi Persei and the 6th magnitude star off the central north side.  The nebula noticeably tapers towards the southeast end as the northern side of this end squeezes inward.  Similarly, the northwest end also tapers as the northern boundary narrows towards the southern side.

13x80mm (2/5/21): very nice view with the 24mm Panoptic and an H-beta filter, as the 5° field frames the 2.5° wide nebula.  Slightly brighter in the middle section, particularly on both the south and north border.

16x80mm (7/27/84): very large and faint, very elongated WNW-ESE, sharper and brighter on WNW edge, very low surface brightness.  Improved contrast with an H-beta filter.

15x50mm IS binoculars (8/27/11): very faintly visible as a large, elongated glow near Xi Persei using a pair of 2" H-beta filters over the objectives.

1x Night-Vision device (11/30/21): with a 6nm H-alpha filter, the California Nebula is a bright, high contrast, very elongated glow.  The Pleiades, nearly 13° to the SSW, shares the same 1x field.

visualUpdates.Name: Sh 2-220
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
14.5" (1/20/25): NVD at 24x; stunning view of the California Nebula, particularly the central section where the southern rim (facing 4th mag Xi Per) is very bright and structured with two nearly parallel, sinewy filaments. The northern filament undulates for ~35', while the southern (outer) filament  extends ~40' and ends close to a mag 7.0 star at its W end.  The N rim is brightest in a thick section further E, though it tapers as it extends SE. The interior is more uniformly lit to the S of this section than other portions. The W end becomes wispy and the N part extending further W quite a ways.  Similarly, there is a very faint extension on the SE end.

NVD at 3x (1/20/25):  Handheld with a 3nm H-alpha filter, the view was even more impressive due to the extra magnification and narrower bandpass filter.  The "tail" was more obvious with this combination.

NVD at 1x with 6nm H-alpha (1/20/25 and 1/25/25): The California Nebula is one of the most prominent NVD targets in the sky at 1x.  I noticed a faint, gently-arcing extension on the east end towards the SE, that seemed to add another degree or so to the length.

NVD at 1x with 6nm H-alpha (11/30/21): the California Nebula appeared as a bright, high contrast, very elongated glow using a handheld 1x image-intensifier monocular.  The Pleiades, nearly 13° to the SSW, shares the same field on the screen.

visualUpdates.Name: PKS 0405-123
visualUpdates.Visual Description: 17.5" (2/3/03): I was able to identify this quasar immediately using 220x in an uncrowded star field.  It appears as a mag 14.5-15 "star" (V = 14.86), and it is situated 2.3' SSW of a mag 11 star and 3.3' NE of a mag 12.5 star. It's visible using direct vision without difficulty. This quasar has a redshift z = .573 (~5.5 billion l.y).

visualUpdates.Name: HCG 33B
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
48" (10/24/11): moderately bright, small, irregularly round, 20"x15".  Very similar appearance to HCG 33A situated 40" S.  HCG 33D lies 1.4' E.  HCG 33C is attached to a mag 13 star situated 0.8' SW.  The entire quartet fits within a 2.5' circle.

17.5" (2/3/03): HCG 33B is the northern of a close pair of galaxies with HCG 33A just 40" S.  It appears faint, very small, elongated 3:2 N-S, roughly 20"x13".  A mag 13.5 star 0.8' SW forms the SW vertex of a small triangle with HCG 33A and 33B.  This galaxy appears slightly brighter and larger than HCG 33A.

visualUpdates.Name: Gamma Lep
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
18" (1/14/08): very bright, very wide pair with mag 3.8 light yellow primary and a mag 6 orange companion at 95"  (very wide even below 100x).

10x30mm IS binoculars: Viewed Gamma Leporum from the beach house.  At a separation of 95", it was easily split with a bright yellow primary and a fainter orange companion.

8": yellow mag 3.8 primary and orange mag 6.2 secondary at a very wide 95".  Splits in 7x50 binoculars and in finder.

visualUpdates.Name: UGC 3431
visualUpdates.Visual Description: 14.5" (1/27/25): at 226x; UGC 3431 is located along a chain of a half-dozen stars including mag 7.8 HD 42330 just 1.4' NE and mag 9.0 HD 42289 2' S!  Despite the nearby bright star, this galaxy is surprisingly bright and was easily seen as the surface brightness in the core region is fairly high.  With a careful look, a diffuse slightly elongated halo surrounds the small, bright core and sharp stellar nucleus.

visualUpdates.Name: Sh 2-308
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
18" (2/4/08): I had a remarkable view of this giant Wolf-Rayet shell at 73x and OIII filter (excellent filter response).  I could trace virtually the complete outline for at least 35' diameter.  The shell was striking along the 25' western border where it gently arcs from north to south with a sharp contrast against the sky immediately to the west.  This region also has some weak filamentary structure and brightness variations.  At the south end of this long arc, the rim curves more sharply east, crossing directly through a triangle of mag 7.5/8/9 stars and dims where it passes just south of 3.9-magnitude 16 CMa.  To the east of 16 CMa, the SE portion of the shell was the only difficult part to follow but it could be picked up again on the eastern edge of the rim.  From this point the rim continues directly north where material appeared to pool up on the north end in a 10' brighter, circular patch.  Superimposed on this obvious glow are a number of mag 10-12 stars.  The rim dimmed again for a short stretch at the NW end before reaching the bright western rim again.  The massive Wolf-Rayet star EZ CMa (mag 6.7-6.9) is at the geometric center of the shell, midway between 16 CMa at the south end (15' separation) and the brighter patch at the north end.  The interior was filled with a very low surface brightness, patchy nebulosity.

18" (3/17/07): at 73x and OIII filter, the western rim of this huge Wolf-Rayet bubble was sharply defined and appeared as a prominent 25' to 30' gently curving arc which began near 3.9-magnitude 16 CMa on the south end and then passed through a trio of mag 8 stars about 10' WNW.  The rim then straightened out, running directly north for at nearly 30', passing through several mag 10 stars.  The nebula appeared fainter along the north side but was evident as a brighter, circular patch that involved a scattered group of mag 10 and fainter stars.  The illuminating, Wolf-Rayet star is 6.7-magnitude EZ CMa, located 15' N of 16 CMa, roughly midway between the brighter patch on the north end and 16 CMa.  The interior appeared filled with a very low surface brightness haze, though due to the size and low contrast, this was difficult to verify.

17.5" (2/1/03 and 2/3/03): this huge, obscure, Wolf-Rayet ring was a surprise at 100x as it appeared as a faint, roughly circular 35'-40' glow just north of naked-eye 16 CMa!  Although faintly visible without a filter, it was quite distinct with an OIII filter, as a very high contrast 25' border running ~N-S along the western border.  This edge is the only portion that shows some structure and irregularities in surface brightness, but it has a pretty dramatic edge (front) with the dark sky to the west.  On the south end, the nebula bends east, crossing through the middle of a trio of mag 7.5-8.5 stars and then passing just south of mag 3.9 16 CMa.  The eastern border fades in brightness and is difficult to trace the edge.  On the northern side there is a locally brighter patch that involves a small group of stars.  The NW corner is sharply angled between the N-S running bright western edge and E-W running northern edge.  Near the center (offset a bit west) is mag 6.7 EZ CMa (mag 6.71-6.95) = HD 50896 = WR 6.  This object responds dramatically to an OIII filter at 63x (31 Nagler), but it is barely visible without a filter. The illuminating star EZ CMa is a massive WR type losing mass from its outer layers through a strong stellar wind.  See observation of Cr 121.

24" (3/17/26): NVD at 34x; vaguely seen using a 6nm H-alpha filter. The view was noticeably improved switching to the dual H-alpha/O III filter. The brighter western rim was clearly visible and well defined. The eastern rim was still vague, but overall the nebula appeared as a huge (35'), low-contrast ring! Mag 3.8 16 CMa is at the S end, with the mag 6.7 WR star EZ CMa at the center.

visualUpdates.Name: Sh 2-309
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
14.5" (3/7/24): NVD at 24x; fairly bright, irregular oval region 10'-12' diameter, situated close NE of mag 7.5 HD 59936. The western side is flattened into an bright N-S running rim, while the eastern side is more diffuse and ragged.  A 9th mag star is embedded at the S end of this streak. The red DSS shows a couple of compact knots involved, but I didn't notice these.  Fainter and much larger Sh 2-306 is roughly 25' NW.  A few OB stars in the embedded cluster Bochum 6 (which didn't stand out) are the ionizing source.

17.5" (2/1/03): At 100x, I immediately noticed a small clump of four stars that seemed weakly nebulous, but there was no responses using an OIII, UHC or H-beta filter.  At 140x, a very small knot was visible on the following side of this small group of stars, but there still was no filter response.  When I increased to 220x the contrast increased further on the nebulous knot and the small clump of stars (~1.5' diameter) seemed encased in a weak nebulous glow, perhaps a couple of arcminutes in size (the listed diameter for Sh 2-309 is 12').  Located 22' WNW of a mag 5.6 HD 60341 and 10' NNE of mag 7.5 SAO 153009.

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 2516
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
13.1" (1/30/06 - Costa Rica): very bright naked-eye cluster located 3° SW of Epsilon Car (southern star in the False Cross).  Appears partially resolved in the 9x50 finder and my 15x50 IS binoculars provided an excellent view.  In the 13.1", the cluster filled over half of the 20mm Nagler field, ~30'-35' diameter with over 100 stars resolved.  The outline is quite irregular though well-detached at low power.  A mag 5.2 M-type giant orange star (V460 = HD 66342) lies at the NE edge of the cluster.  The central region is more concentrated and uniform and includes a number of tinted yellow or orange stars.  A nice triple star (HJ 4027 = 7.1/7.8/9.3 at 9" and 20") is on the W edge of the cluster and an excellent double (HJ 4031 = 7.2/8.0 at 5") lies on the E side of the cluster.  A long curving string starts in the center and heads NE to the mag 5.2 orange star.  This string includes a 9" evenly matched pair of mag 9 stars (Innes 1104) that was resolved at low power.  Mag 5.7 K-type orange subgiant HD 65662 is off the NW side of the cluster.

13.1" (2/17/04 - Costa Rica): this bright naked-eye cluster is located SW of the "False Cross" (3 degrees SW of 2nd-magnitude Epsilon Carinae) and is the only open cluster in western Carina.  It was well resolved in the 9x50 finder.  At 105x, the main group is 25'-30' with outliers increasing the size and roughly 100 stars are resolved including a number of mag 6-8 stars.  Many of the stars are arranged in loops and strings and overall the cluster is quite irregular in magnitudes and star distributions.  There is a close, fairly bright double on the SE side (7.2/8.0 at 5.5") and a neat 13' chain of stars near the west side running N-S.

10x30mm Canon IS binocs (7/10/02 - Magellan Observatory, Australia): this is a prominent naked-eye cluster below the "False Cross" (formed by Epsilon and Iota Car as well as Delta and Kappa Vel), on a line with the longer axis (Epsilon Car and Kappa Vel) of the cross.  In binoculars, it appeared well-resolved, ~50' diameter including outliers with 5 bright stars (mag 6.5-7.5) with a couple of dozen stars resolved overall.  Appears fairly rich towards the center with a number of mag 8-10 stars.

10x30mm Canon IS binocs (3/28/19 - Tasmania): very bright naked-eye cluster, gorgeous even at 10x with a couple of dozen stars resolved, 40'-50' diameter, many brighter stars around the periphery, but richer towards the center.

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 3034
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
48" (4/15/10): stunning view at 330x with numerous irregular dark rifts slicing up the mottled, clumpy surface.  Several very small, bright knots or condensations (Super Star Clusters - SSCs) are just west of a dark wedge that pierces the galaxy on the south side and tapers as it cuts across the center at an oblique angle.  The very bright section of the galaxy to the northeast of the dark absorption wedge also displays mottled structure.  Another prominent dark inclusion cuts into the galaxy from the north on the northeast side of the galaxy.  A very faint extension of low surface brightness haze (the superwind outflow) bulges out from the main portion of the galaxy on the south side.  This glow is west of the dark wedge and east of a mag 10.5 star located 5.8' SW of center. On images this large bulge appears to explode out from the galaxy with filamentary structure.  Overall, there was too much visible structure to describe from a couple of minutes at the eyepiece.

24" (1/25/14): viewed type-Ia SN 2014J (discovered 4 days earlier), which was close to 11th magnitude and apparently still brightening. It appeared a pale orange or red color!  I don't know if this was due to intervening dust in M82, but I hadn't seen this effect before in a supernova.  This is the closest type-Ia discovered in the past 42 years.

17.5" (10/12/85): very bright, large, edge-on 4:1 WSW-ENE, 10' x 2.5', large bright irregular core.  Very mottled with an unusually high surface brightness.  Unique appearance with several dark cuts oblique to the major axis including a prominent wedge or cut nearly through the center.  A mag 10 star is just south of the SW end 5.8' from the center

13.1" (4/24/82 and 11/5/83): highly mottled with two obvious dark lanes.

8": bright, spindle, mottled.  A dark wedge cuts into the galaxy near the center from the south side.

10x50mm binoculars: faintly visible though easier in 15x50mm binos..

visualUpdates.Name: Sextans B
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
48" (4/18/15): Sextans B is a nearby dwarf galaxy, generally considered to lie just outside the local group in a small group that also includes Sextans A.  It appeared as a large, fairly low surface brightness oval glow, extending 4:3 WNW-ESE, ~2.6'x1.9'.  It exhibited a broad weak concentration to a slightly brighter middle, but there was no distinct core or zones.  The surface brightness appeared irregular and slightly clumpy.  A mag 14.5 star is at the north edge of the galaxy and a mag 15 star is off the southeast edge of the galaxy.

A young (2 ± 1 billion years) massive globular cluster (SDSS J100004.63+052007.5) was discovered in 2007 in Sextans B using the HST WFPC2 and verified at the Special Astrophysical Observatory in Russia.  At V = 17.9 it appeared as an extremely faint "star" and was visible only intermittently, though was repeatedly confirmed at the same position.  This GC is located ~1.2' ENE of the center of Sextans B, close to the east edge of the galaxy.

18" (2/19/09): easily visible at 175x as a large, low surface brightness, oval patch, extended 3:2 NW-SE, ~3.0'x1.9'.  The glow is nearly parallel to two mag 13 stars off the NE side and extends roughly the separation of these stars (3').  This dwarf galaxy has only a broad, weak concentration with a slightly brighter core and an ill-defined edge to the halo as it fades at the periphery.  Still, the surface brightness is slightly irregular with a hint of mottling.  Located 8' NE of mag 7.7 HD 86610.

17.5" (2/1/03): This dwarf irregular galaxy probably lies just outside the local group (4.3 million l.y.) in a small group that includes NGC 3109, Sextans A and the Antlia Dwarf.  I picked up Sextans B at 100x without difficulty, just 8' NE of mag 7.7 SAO 118040.  Increasing to 140x, Sextans B appeared as a large, oval glow, elongated 3:2 WNW-ESE, and spanning about 3.5'x2.2'. The galaxy has a low surface brightness and only a broad, weak concentration.  The surface seems slightly irregular or mottled and four fainter stars are near the periphery.  Overall, the observation was surprisingly easy though I had never searched for it before

visualUpdates.Name: Hewett 1
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
4" (6/10/26): NVD at 8x with a 3nm H-alpha filter; Mark McCarthy found this huge planetary nebula (or more likely ionized ISM from the white dwarf PG 1034+001) near the galaxy NGC 3325 and called me over for a look. I verified the brightest part within a trapezium of mag 10-12 stars by flipping between an untiltered view and the 3nm H-alpha filter. It appeared as a faint, elongated glow perhaps 15'-18' in diameter.

Paul Hewett et al. discovered this object in 2003 on the SDSS.

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 3310
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
14.5" (8/8/26): the bright SN 2026sqf appeared at mag ~11.6, and was quite impressive, despite the galaxy only at 20° altitude at the end of astronomical twilight. 

24" (7/12/26 and 7/14/26): at 329x; contains a very bright core with a stellar nucleus. The core is surrounded by much lower surface brightness halo. Type II SN 2026sqf, discovered 4 days earlier, is a surprisingly bright mag 12.8 "star" (still rising), situated 29" NE of center, just outside the prominent core. At 457x; the core had an uneven texture and was slightly brighter on the NE side near the supernova (where the northern spiral arm attaches)

48" (5/16/12): extremely bright, fairly large, sharply concentrated with a large, very bright, slightly elongated N-S core, ~1' diameter.  The core appears mottled with a couple of "stellarings" or small knots.  The core is surrounded by a larger, much lower surface brightness irregular halo, extending the central portion to nearly 2'.  An outer spiral arm is attached on the north side of the halo and was most evident near the halo.  Occasionally, a very large, very low surface brightness looping arm was glimpsed, rotating 180° clockwise and ending west of the core, ~1.7' from center.

14.5" (4/12/21): bright, moderately large, roundish, sharply concentrated with a relatively large, very bright core that dominates the galaxy and a smaller, much fainter halo.  The core has a slightly elongated uneven surface brightness.  A nag 12 star is 3' N and mag 5.5 HD 92095 is 10' NNE.

17.5" (1/19/91): very bright, moderately large.  Unusual appearance as contains a very bright, very large central core with uniform high surface brightness with only a very faint, fairly small halo, elongated NW-SE.  Located 10.4' SSW of mag 5.5 HR 4165 at the edge of the 220x field.  A mag 12 star lies 3.0' N.

visualUpdates.Name: Rose 3
visualUpdates.Visual Description: 48" (5/15/26): at 610x; the Rose 3 quartet is only 1.2' across, with all members between V = 16.4 to 16.7. They all appeared faint or very faint and about 10" each in diameter.  The group lies about 1.25 Gly away, though one galaxy has a closer distance of 1.1 Gly based on redshift.

visualUpdates.Name: Mel 111
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
8x50mm finder: scattered group of about 30 stars mag 5 and fainter in a 5° field.  The brightest in mag 4.8 12 Com. Also excellent in 7x50mm and 10x50mm IS binoculars.

Naked-eye (numerous dates): Very easy in reasonably dark skies with a number of the brighter stars (11 stars down to mag 5.7) visible naked-eye.

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 5139
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
25" (3/29/25 - OzSky): at 187x; the view felt three-dimensional with a fantastically rich field of sharp stars from edge to edge stretching across 26'.

24" (4/11/08 - Magellan Observatory, Australia): at 200x in excellent seeing, the view was absolutely stunning as the field was packed with thousands of pinpoint stars to the edge of the 30' field!  I noted the circular ring of stars near the center mentioned previously, but the large number of brighter, densely packed stars in the core and halo, superimposed on an incredibly rich mat of fainter stars was the real show.  The cluster is only broadly concentrated with very large, brighter core ~10' in diameter and the star density thins out very slowly all the way to 35' diameter.

20" (7/08/02 - Magellan Observatory, Australia): at 208x with a 24' field, the cluster overfilled the field with edge to edge stars mag 11.5 and fainter and was a breathtaking sight.  Broadly concentrated with large, brighter core of at least 10' in diameter.  The core is extremely densely packed with layers of stars.  The elongated halo gradually thins but has no definite border out to 30'!  This is the largest and brightest globular in the sky (V = 3.7) and an obvious naked-eye blur, but lacks the strong central condensation of NGC 104 = 47 Tucana.

18" (7/10/05 - Magellan Observatory, Australia): although I've mentioned this feature on previous observations I was surprised to be drawn to a 1' circular ring of stars just north of the geometric center which is mainly filled with unresolved glow and appears like a darker "hole" near the center.  A second smaller and less distinct 30" ring of stars and darker center is adjacent to the south with the two rings externally tangent in the middle.

After the observation I checked John Herschel's description and found these comments on the star rings in the center: "One of these rings, 1.5' in diameter, is so marked as to give the appearance of a comparative darkness like a hole in the centre.  My attendant (J.S.) called up, who saw the hole and darkness, and described it as I have done above. On further attention the hole is double, or an oval space crossed by a bridge of stars. Position of axis = 150."

13.1" (2/20/04 - Costa Rica): at 105x in excellent seeing, the view was absolutely breathtaking with wall-to-wall pinpoint stars in the 37' field!  There was a clear 3-dimensional effect with the 11.5-12.5 magnitude stars seemingly floating over a dense mat of fainter stars with the streamers in the halo reaching the edges of the field. I don't recall a more impressive view in the 12" from Australia, where the cluster was higher in the sky. 

13.1" (2/19/04 - Costa Rica): In very good seeing early in the morning of the 20th, Omega Cen was a mesmerizing sea of a couple of thousand stars at 200x.  I set Omega just outside the field and let it drift through the field a few times.  The outer halo was an amazingly dense swarm of 12-13th magnitude stars over a background of fainter pinpoints of lights spilling over the edge of the field.  Very broadly concentrated to a large, brighter center although there is no well-defined core.

12.2" (6/29/02 - Bargo, Australia): this was the first object I viewed at Bargo with Les Dalrymple's 12" and I was not disappointed.  At 140x, it filled 2/3 of the field (over 25') and resolved into perhaps a few thousand stars down to the center.  The cluster seemed almost 3-dimensional with a lattice of brighter mag 12 stars superimposed on a dense background layer of mag 13-14 stars.  The density was generally uniformly high in the elongated halo except near the edge although the core shows more non-uniformity with a couple of darker patches.

17.5" (3/12/88): very large, very bright, fantastic at 220x with several hundred stars resolved in excellent seeing from east of Mt. Hamilton.  Very faintly visible to the naked eye in good conditions near the horizon from northern California.  

13.1" (3/24/84): large, mottled disc covered with faint stars, well resolved outer halo.  Similar view but even better resolution on 2/23/85.

8" (7/13/91 - Southern Baja): very bright, very large, very broadly concentrated, about 25' diameter, over 100 stars resolved mag 12-13, many in curving streams over the entire disc.  Visible naked-eye.

10x30mm Canon IS (3/28/19 - Tasmania): very prominent naked-eye as Omega Centauri culminated within 5° of the zenith from this southern location.  Huge in 10x30mm, though no resolution.

NVD at 1x (6/10/26): using an IR-pass filter, Omega Cen was a very small, prominent glow with a handheld NVD, although the cluster was barely above the horizon at an elevation of 3°.

visualUpdates.Name: HCG 69A
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
48" (5/17/26): at 488x; between fairly faint and moderately bright, edge-on 4:1 SW-NE, ~60"x15". Contains a very small brighter nucleus.  HCG 69D is at the W edge, 20" between centers, and HCG 69C is ~40" E of center.

17.5" (4/13/96): this galaxy is the brightest member of HCG 69 group (triple system).  Very faint, small, elongated 2:1 E-W, very low even surface brightness.  Requires averted vision and concentration to see elongation clearly. HCG 69B lies 1.5' SE.  Located 4.5' ENE of brighter IC 4345.

17.5" (6/8/96): HCG 69A was resolved from extremely faint HCG 69C which forms the third of the triple system just 0.6' following.  Surrounded by a cluster of faint IC galaxies and viewed IC's 4342, 4343, 4344, 4345, 4346, 4348, 4349.

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 5499
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
24" (7/10/26): at 327x and 375x; fairly faint, elongated ~5:3 NNW-SSE, ~45" diameter, mild concentration with a brighter core.  CGCG 191-61, situated 8' ESE, appeared faint, slightly elongated 4:3, low surface brightness, brighter core.

17.5" (6/2/00): faint, small, elongated 4:3 NNW-SSE?, weak broad concentration, occasional faint stellar nucleus.  A wide pair of mag 11/13 stars lies 3' SSE. NGC 5517 is 28' SE.

visualUpdates.Name: IC 4382
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
48" (5/17/26): at 488x; fairly bright, high surface brightness, very thin edge-on 5:1 N-S, 0.6'x0.12' in length, brighter along the major axis. IC 4381 is 1.8' SW.

17.5" (6/8/96): faint, fairly small, elongated nearly 3:1 N-S, 0.8'x0.3'.  Higher surface brightness than larger IC 4381 = HCG 71A 1.8' SW.

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 5548
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
24" (7/14/26): at 327x; bright, round, ~1.25' diameter, sharply concentrated with a very bright small core and an intense stellar nucleus. CGCG 133-24 is 10' SW and UGC 9165 is 16' SE.

13.1" (6/4/83): fairly bright, small, fairly bright stellar nucleus [Seyfert galaxy], round, faint halo.  Brightest in a small group (LGG 381) with NGC 5559 26' SE.

visualUpdates.Name: UGC 9165
visualUpdates.Visual Description: 24" (7/14/26): at 327x; faint, thin edge-on, ~5:1 SW-NE, brighter core.  Forms a pair with CGCG 133-031 3.1' E. Member of the NGC 5548 group (LGG 381)

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 5559
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
24" (7/14/26): at 327x; fairly faint, very elongated 3:1 or 4:1 WSW-ENE, brighter bulging core.  UGC 9165, located 10' NW, is a faint, thin edge-on, ~5:1 SW-NE, brighter core. A 16th mag star is 1' E.

13.1" (6/4/83): very faint, elongated WSW-ENE, fairly small, requires averted vision.  NGC 5548 lies 26' NW (similar redshifts).

visualUpdates.Name: UGC 9244
visualUpdates.Visual Description: 24" (6/15/26): at 327x; fairly faint, elongated ~5:3 N-S, diffuse halo, brighter core, ~1' x0.6'.

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 5639
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
24" (7/14/26): at 327x; fairly faint, low surface brightness oval glow, elongated 5:3 E-W. A mag 11.8 star is 1' S of center. Situated 3.8' ESE of mag 8.0 HD 127066, which detracts from the view. Improved with star placed outside of field.

17.5" (6/5/99): faint, moderately large, round, low surface brightness, no concentration, slightly elongated E-W.  A mag 11.5 star is just 0.9' S of center.  Located 3.8' ESE of mag 8 SAO 64162, which detracts from viewing.

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 5642
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
24" (7/14/26): at 327x; moderately bright, elongated ~5:3 NW-SE, ~1.2'x0.8', strong concentration with a low surface brightness halo. A star is attached at the ESE edge of the core and a mag 12.3 star is 1.5' E.  CGCG 163-062, situated just 3.0' N, is faint, fairly small, nearly round, low even surface brightness, easily visible.

17.5" (6/5/99): fairly faint, moderately large, elongated 3:2 WNW-ESE, small bright core, 1.2'x0.8'.  A mag 13 star is attached on the following side 18" from center.  A mag 12 follows by 1.5'.

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 5646
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
24" (7/14/26): at 327x; between faint and fairly faint, very elongated 3:1 WSW-ENE, 1.0' in length, slightly brighter elongated core. A mag 10.2 star, aligned with the major axis, is 1.8' ENE.  UGC 9315 (double) is 7.2' NNE.

17.5" (6/20/98): very faint, small.  With extended viewing, elongated 3:1 WSW-ENE, 1.0'x0.3', only a weak concentration.  Requires averted to see full extensions well.  The major axis is collinear with a mag 10 star 2.0' following. Located 13' NW of NGC 5656.

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 5656
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
24" (7/14/26): at 327x and 457x; fairly bright, oval 4:3 SW-NE, 60"x45", slightly brighter core.

17.5" (6/20/98): moderately bright, fairly small, elongated 3:2 SW-NE, 1.2'x0.8'.  The brighter core is moderately concentrated.  Located 3.9' WNW of mag 9.5 SAO 64190.  A mag 14 star lies 1.0' SSE.  NGC 5646 is located 13' NW, just outside the 220x field.

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 5673
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
24" (7/10/26): at 327x; fairly faint, edge-on 4:1 NW-SE, 2.0'x0.5'. A brighter core is slightly bulging and the tips slightly taper.  A 13th-mag star is barely off the NW end. Overall, the surface brightness is moderately low and NGC5683 appears fainter than IC 1029, which is 10' ESE.

17.5" (6/24/95): faint, edge-on 5:1 NW-SE, 2.2'x0.4'.  NGC 5673 has similar dimensions and position angle as IC 1029 9.7' ESE but doesn't contain a bright core so is not nearly as prominent in the same field.  A mag 13.5 star is at the NW tip 1.1' from center.  IC 1029 = UGC 9361 appeared moderately bright, edge-on 5:1 NNW-SSE, 2.0'x0.4'.  Contains a very small and round prominent core with a faint stellar nucleus at moments.

8" (7/10/26): at 109x; very dim elongated glow with a very low even surface brightness. A mag 13 star is at the NW end.

visualUpdates.Name: STF 1855
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
24" (7/14/26): at 327x; wide mag 9.2/9.9 pair at 16" with a third mag 14.5 star ("C") nearly on a line to the WSW at 18" from the secondary ("B")/

14.5" (6/20/22): routine 16" pair at 66x with fairly small 0.7 delta.  The 10th mag secondary was fairly faint in a bright sky.

17.5" (6/20/98): NGC 5672 is located  4' NE of a striking evenly matched double star STF 1855 = 9.2/10.1 at 15".  The major axis of the galaxy is nearly collinear with this double star!

visualUpdates.Name: IC 1029
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
24" (7/10/26): at 327x; fairly bright, edge-on at least 4:1 NW-SE. Sharp concentration with a roundish, bright core and a stellar-like nucleus. A 10th-mag star is 3.2' E.  IC 1029 is the brighter of a pair of edge-ons with NGC 5673 10' WNW.

17.5" (6/24/95): moderately bright, edge-on 5:1 NNW-SSE, 2.0'x0.4'.  Contains a very small and round prominent core with a faint stellar nucleus at moments.  Located 3.2' W of a mag 9.5 star.  This is an unusual situation with a brighter IC galaxy (discovered by William Herschel) in the field of a fainter NGC galaxy (discovered by John Herschel).

8" (7/10/26): at 109x; faint, very elongated NW-SE, dominated by a small bright core.

visualUpdates.Name: UGC 9444
visualUpdates.Visual Description: 24" (6/15/26): at 327x; relatively bright UGC, roundish, strong concentration with a bright core that increases to a strong nucleus, ~45" diameter.  Situated 3.4' E of a 9th mag star.

visualUpdates.Name: Mrk 820
visualUpdates.Visual Description: 24" (7/14/26): at 327x; faint, small, round, ~20" diameter. Occasionally a very small nucleus appears somewhat brighter. Situated 15' WSW of 8th mag HD 129355 (RW Boo).

visualUpdates.Name: IC 1028
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
See observing notes for NGC 5739. UGC 9368 is identified as IC 1028 in modern catalogues.

24" (6/14/26): this galaxy is attached to a mag 12.6 star, which affects viewing. At 327x; faint, elongated 2:1 or 3:1 N-S, ~0.7'x0.3', appears as a faint streak on the W side of the star.

visualUpdates.Name: WBL 524
visualUpdates.Visual Description: 48" (5/16/12): 8 galaxies with brightest members UGC 9621, UGC 9523, MCG +02-38-007, MCG +02-38-007, MCG +02-38-008, CGCG 076-040.  These should all be easily visible in the 18".

visualUpdates.Name: UGCA 394
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
24" (6/13/26): at 202x; very faint, extremely thin edge-on ~6:1 N-S, ~2' x 20", slightly brighter core.  Three wide pairs of stars forming two parallel rows are NW and NE of the galaxy.

BU 346, a pair of mag 7.5/7.9 stars at 2.8" separation is 17' NE.

visualUpdates.Name: BU 346
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
14.5" (6/4/26): excellent 2.8" pair with well matched mag 7.5/7.9 components. Resolved cleanly at 158x.

14.5" (6/18/21): Very nice well matched pair (delta V = 0.4) of mag 7.5/7.9 stars at 2.7" separation.  Resolved at 158x.

UGCA 394 is 17' WSW.

visualUpdates.Name: VV 130
visualUpdates.Visual Description: 24" (6/13/26): at 202x; faint, diffuse, elongated ~2:1 NW-SE, ~1.2'x0.6'.  Located 13' NW of mag 7.6 HD 130991.

visualUpdates.Name: CGCG 164-036
visualUpdates.Visual Description: 24" (7/14/26): at 327x; faint (viewed 4.5 hrs past the meridian), elongated 2:1 SW-NE, fairly low even surface brightness. Aligned with a mag 12.9 star 3.4' SE and a mag 14.1 star 2.3' NW.  This galaxy is the brightest member of the galaxy cluster Abell 1982.

visualUpdates.Name: STT 288
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
14.5" (6/6/26): tight 0.85" pair of mag 6.9/7.6. The components were split at 264x with a noticeable black gap at 395x, even in average seeing.

24" (4/17/26): at 375x; very close split, but separated in fair seeing.  There is some scattered light due to the brightness of the components, which are fairly well balanced.

6.5" (5/14/88): STT 288 is currently at 1.3" separation. It was resolved in good seeing using an off-axis mask with the 17.5".

visualUpdates.Name: UGC 9633
visualUpdates.Visual Description: 24" (6/15/26): UGC 9633 is an interacting pair at nearly 700 Mly. At 327x, I immediately noticed a faint, round glow, ~20" diameter, situated very close SW of a 14th mag star.  With careful viewing a second very faint glow, only ~12" diameter, was seen 0.4' SSW. The cores are separated by 22".

visualUpdates.Name: IC 1101
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
18" (6/30/11): this supergiant cD galaxy is the central galaxy in AGC 2029 (z = .078 at 1.0 billion light years!).  At 280x, it appeared very faint, very small, slightly elongated ~N-S, ~15"x10".  Visible continuously with averted vision.  The galaxy is centered within a 9-member circlet of 12th- to 14th-magnitude stars and squeezed between a mag 14.7 star 27" E and a mag 15-15.5 star 47" WNW (just slightly south of a line connecting these stars).  No other members of the cluster were seen.  

24" f/3.3 (6/30/11): faint, very small, oval 3:2 N-S, ~20"x14".  Could just hold steadily with direct vision.

Wikipedia states this galaxy is the largest known in the universe, from 5-6 million light years.  A 1991 paper by Uson, Boughn, & Kuhn (ApJ, 369, 46) gives a slightly smaller, though still extremely large diameter of 4 million light years.

visualUpdates.Name: IC 1116
visualUpdates.Visual Description: 18" (7/28/03): fairly faint, moderately large, slightly elongated N-S, 1.0'x0.8'.  Contains a very small brighter core.  Located 4.5' ESE of mag 8.7 SAO 120958 and ~15' SW of the rich core of AGC 2063.  This galaxy is the brightest member of AGC 2063 although it is ~20' southwest of the center of the cluster.  UGC 09821 lies 3' W.

visualUpdates.Name: STT 298
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
14.5" (8/1/26): excellent close 1.1" pair of mag 7.2/8.4 stars. They are fairly bright and only a moderate delta V of 1.3.  I was able to resolve the pair fairly readily at 330x. The C components is a mag 7.7 star at an extremely wide 2' away.

24" (6/13/15): The pair was cleanly split at 375x into two sharp discs.  Picked up without prior knowledge while observing NGC 5966.  In fact, it was not printed on my Megastar chart as the separation was only 0.3" in 1997.

The "D" component of the system is the galaxy NGC 5966.

visualUpdates.Name: He 2-131
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
18" (7/10/05 - Magellan Observatory, Australia): viewing unfiltered at 128x, the mag 11 central star was identified, but there was no obvious halo.  At 228x (still unfiltered), a very small 4" or so halo was visible around the star.  The halo was most evident using averted vision and the tiny halo disappeared using direct vision (similar to the Blinking Planetary).

He 2-131 is a low excitation planetary that should respond to an H-beta filter and display a reddish halo in good conditions.  The listed magnitude of 11.7 includes the central star.  Located 4.7' NNE of a mag 10 star.

visualUpdates.Name: Barnard 228
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
15x50mm binoculars (6/28/06 - Hawaii): excellent elongated dark lane in 15x50 IS binoculars.  Extends up to 4° by 20' running NW to SE, passing just north of mag 4.7 Psi 1 and Psi 2 Lupi (separation 40') and reaching a 15' pair of mag 5.8/6.9 stars at the southeast end.  The dark lane is mostly devoid of stars.  This Barnard object stands out fairly well though I expected a more dramatic contrast.

Barnard described "This vacant region is about 4° long, extending from a = 15h 43m, d = -35°30'. Its average width is about 1/2°. It is strongest marked at the north end. There are fragments of other dark markings several degrees west of this."

visualUpdates.Name: UGC 10020
visualUpdates.Visual Description: 24" (6/15/26): at 327x; faint, round diffuse glow with a low nearly even surface brightness, diameter of 1'. A group of 5 stars is to the west and an 11th mag star is 4' E.

visualUpdates.Name: HS 1549+1919
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
24" (6/14/26): at 375x; using three bright stars in the field, I identified three mag 13.8/14.2/14.6 stars that form a right triangle very close to this z = 2.843 quasar (light-travel time 11.4 billion years). The quasar appeared as a faint 16th mag star about half the time with averted vision.

When the quasar emitted this light, it was only ~5.3 billion light-years away in proper distance; cosmic expansion has stretched that separation to ~20 billion light-years at the present time.

visualUpdates.Name: STT 303
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
14.5" (8/1/26): although I had just resolved STT 298 at 1.2" separation just previously without problem, this 1.6" pair was often merged at 330x. When the seeing sharpened, the mag 7.7/8.1 components were clearly resolved, though only briefly.

24" (7/18/15): cleanly resolved at 375x when the seeing settles.  The two components are fairly bright and reasonably well matched (delta V = 0.4).

visualUpdates.Name: STT 304
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
14.5" (8/1/26): very unbalanced 11" pair of mag 6.8/10.6 stars, but easily split at 132x with a comfortable separation.

18" (7/1/10): easy, large mag contrast pair at 175x with a bright (mag 6.8), white primary and a mag 10.5 companion at 10" separation.

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 6093
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
24" (7/4/24): beautiful symmetric globular with a blazing core and nucleus and a highly resolved halo that extends up to 6'. Roughly 100 stars are visible at 327x. The core is densely packed and resists resolution, but a quite a few faint stars are layered over the center, several popping on and off.  A mag 8.5 star is a bit off the NE edge of the halo. Two nearby faint galaxies were viewed: ESO 516-010 (often identified as IC 4600) 17' NW and IC 4596 25' NNW.

18" (7/24/06): at 325x appears bright, fairly large, round, pretty symmetrical appearance, contains a blazing 1.5' core in a 5' to 6' halo.  At 435x the halo and the periphery of the core are well resolved into roughly 100 stars and additional extremely faint stars pop in and out of visibility.  The core itself is overlayed with a number of faint stars.  Beautiful view at 565x as the cluster nearly fills the 7' field with 100-150 stars from edge to edge and the core region is well resolved.  The cluster appears asymmetric with the halo more extensive to the west (core offset to the east). Mag 8.5 HD 146457 is at the NE edge of the halo.

17.5" (6/3/00): fairly bright, round, 5' diameter, well concentrated with a bright 1.5' core and an intense 30" nucleus.  At 500x, the nucleus is clearly offset east of center and the outer halo is well resolved into at least 75 stars.  A dim galaxy, IC 4596, lies 25' NW.

13.1" (7/5/83): contains a small intense unresolved core surrounded by fairly compact halo 5' diameter.  The nucleus is offset to the east within the halo.  The outer halo resolves into a few dozen faint stars over haze. 

8" (7/5/83): a few faint stars resolve at moderate to high power at edges, very grainy, difficult to resolve.

visualUpdates.Name: VV 129d
visualUpdates.Visual Description: 48" (4/5/13): the faintest component of the UGC 10321 quadruple system was not seen at 375x in soft seeing.

visualUpdates.Name: UGC 10319
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
48" (5/21/23): at 488x; HCG 81A is faint to fairly faint, slightly elongated N-S, 0.3'x0.2', low surface brightness.  Situated at the N end of the small HCG 81 quartet with HCG 81D 30" SSE.  HCG 81D is the NWern of a very close pair with 81C just 9" NW.  They were both very faint, round, ~8" diameter.  A 17th mag star (best seen at 610x) is 9" NE of 81D. HCG 81B is faint to fairly faint, round, 12" diameter. Situated at the S end of the N-S chain. HCG 81C is 0.3' NE.

24" (7/6/13): HCG 81A appeared as an extremely faint to very faint knot, very small, round, 12" diameter, stellar nucleus.  This galaxy is at the N end of the small HCG 81 quartet, and it forms the SE vertex of an equilateral triangle with two mag 12.5/13 stars 2.5' N and WNW.

HCG 81B is at the south end of the chain. It appeared very faint, extremely small, round, 10" diameter. HCG 81 C/D is as a single, unresolved glow 35" SSE of HCG 81A. It is a very faint and small, irregularly round, ~12" diameter.  CGCG 80-2 (brighter than the individual components of HCG 81) lies 5' S.

24" (6/16/12): HCG 81A and similar 81B were the only two members of this extremely compact quartet that were clearly resolved at times.  At 322x, both appeared extremely faint and small, round, 8" diameter.  Although not resolved, HCG 81C and D appeared as an extremely faint glow ~20" NNE of 81B and the "clump" of 81B/C/D was more evident than 81A. The entire quartet spans 51" N-S with 81A at the north end and 81B at the south end.  Two mag 12.5 stars 2.5' NNW and 2.5' WNW form an equilateral triangle with the group and are helpful with pinpointing the location.

18" (8/3/05): at 257x an extremely faint, small, low surface brightness glow was intermittently visible perhaps 1/3 of the time.  Forms the southern vertex of an equilateral triangle with two mag 12.5 to the WNW and NNW.  Only a single member or the combined glow of two or more members was seen.

17.5" (8/22/98): using a GSC finder chart, either HCG 81A or the combined glow of two or more galaxies was seen as an extremely faint glow.  At moments it appeared elongated or possibly double, though observation was difficult in windy conditions.  Forms the southern vertex of an equilateral triangle with two mag 12.5 stars 2.7' N and 2.7' NW.

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 6144
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
18" (7/26/06): at 325x roughly two dozen stars were resolve over an irregular, scraggly glow. A mag 12 star at the west edge is probably a field star.  Very weak central condensation (concentration class XI). so the appearance does not look like a typical globular.

17.5" (6/6/86): about 20 stars mag 12-14 resolve at 286x.  The brightest mag 12 star is at the west edge.  Located 37' NW of Antares.  This globular is about 30,000 light years away or 5 times the distance of nearby M4. 

13.1" (6/18/85): a dozen very faint stars resolve at 220x over haze.  Includes a string of stars to the SE.

13.1" (6/19/82): just resolves in steady moments into perhaps 15 very faint stars over haze.  Otherwise the globular is very lively and mottled.

8" (6/5/81): faint, small.  A mag 12 star is at the SW end but no other resolution.  Located 40' NW of Antares.

visualUpdates.Name: Antares
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
8" (7/14/26): easy split when the seeing settled at 229x.

24" (4/11/08 - Magellan Observatory, Australia): cleanly resolved at 200x and well separated at 350x.

18" (7/12/07): split cleanly using the 6" mask at 225x, though close at this magnification.

18" (6/25/04): Antares' blue-green companion was visible continuously at 300x, although there was a great deal of scattered light from Antares.  The companion was also visible (cleaner view but hard to pick out companion) with the 6-inch mask at 300x.  The most satisfying view was probably with the 6-inch mask at 215x.  Period of ~900 years.

17.5" (7/31/00): Antares was split cleanly at 280x.

6.75" (6/6/86): using an off-axis mask on the 17.5" Antares was cleanly resolved at 286x with the fainter companion an apparent greenish color.

8" (6/5/80 and 3/13/81): requires very steady conditions to split, but resolves at 220x.

6" (7/25/09): fairly clean view using the 6" mask at 300x.  Once identified close west of Antares, it was nearly visible continuously though mostly dancing around.

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 6235
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
24" (8/29/19): unusual observation of NGC 6235 with Jupiter just 8' of the globular and Callisto superimposed on the outer south portion of the halo of the globular!  Using 260x, with Jupiter off the edge of the field and Callisto resolved as an obvious 1.3" disc, the core of NGC 6235 is a small, hazy patch and the halo is occasionally seen as a low surface brightness glow.

18" (7/24/06): at 435x this globular is quite scraggly with a small, irregularly shaped core surrounded by a much fainter low surface brightness halo extending to 3'-3.5' diameter.  At least 15 to 20 stars are resolved with 3 or 4 fairly easy brighter stars but most are very faint, in the mag 15-16 range.  With extended viewing, several extremely faint stars pop in and out of visibility in the halo, increasing the overall total to 25-30 stars, though a lower number were visible simultaneously.

17.5" (6/8/91): fairly bright, small, 3' diameter, mottled.  A few stars resolve at the edges of the halo including a fairly prominent mag 14 star at the east edge of the halo and another mag 14 star at the west edge of the core.  The remaining resolved stars are mag 15 or fainter.  The core is elongated N-S.  The globular has an irregular scraggly halo due to unresolved star lanes.  Located within a triangle of three mag 12-13 stars.

visualUpdates.Name: Sh 2-2
visualUpdates.Visual Description: NVD at 1x (6/13/26): Sh 2-2 appeared as a faint, very large, roundish diffuse glow 2-3° in diameter. Situated ~2.8° NE of IC 4628 (Prawn Nebula), which has a high surface brightness with a H-alpha filter.

visualUpdates.Name: Sh 2-5
visualUpdates.Visual Description: NVD at 1x (6/10/26): Using a 7nm H-alpha filter, Sh 2-5 appeared as a very large, faint, ill-defined glow to the NE of more obvious Sh 2-2. Both of these H II regions are between the Prawn Nebula (IC 4628) and the Cat's Paw Nebula (NGC 6334).

visualUpdates.Name: Sh 2-8
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
NVD at 1x (6/13/26): I noticed that even at 1x, the Cat's Paw Nebula appeared noticeably elongated NW to SE.

NVD at 3x (6/10/26): Using a 3nm H-alpha filter and a monopod, NGC 6334 (Cat's Paw Nebula) formed a prominent pair of irregular, high surface brightness nebulae (both at least 1/2° across) with NGC 6357 (War and Peace Nebula).  The pair is oriented SW-NE, with NGC 6334 on the SW side.  I also viewed this region at 1x handheld using a 7nm H-alpha filter and both nebulae stood out prominently in the field.

14.5" (8/11/23): NVD at 24x; Eight sections of the Cat's Paw Nebula were identified. A rough diagram I made through the NVD matched up very well with H-alpha images!  In order of brightness:
1) Southwest "Paw" = Gum 61.  This is the brightest individual piece in the Cat's Paw.  The rim forms a nearly perfect "Horseshoe" shape that was locally brightest along the flatter base of the horseshoe.
2) Southeast "Paw" = Gum 62.  U-shaped, fairly similar to 1), but not filled in as much in the interior.  A brighter star (mag 9.4 HD 156738) is superposed, roughly at the focus of the curve.
3) East "Paw" = Gum 64B.  Situated direction north of Paw 2), it appeared more like a triangular wedge with a nearly stellar knot at one vertex.  It was slightly brighter along the eastern edge and involves the open cluster vdB-Ha 223.
4) Northern "Paw": thin wedge or finger of nebulosity, a few stars are involved.  A N-S oriented dark lane (#8) sharply cuts off the eastern edge.
5) Central knot = Gum 64A: small elongated knot in the center.
6) Surprisingly large diffuse nebulosity extending west and northwest, at least as large as the combined region of the "Paws".  The SW portion (north of section 1) is fainter and more diffuse.  Labeleled as 7) on my diagram.  This region is catalogued as Gum 63 with possible ionizing O8-type star HD 319702.

visualUpdates.Name: Sh 2-11
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
NVD at 3x (6/10/26): Using a 3nm H-alpha filter and a monopod, NGC 6357 (War and Peace Nebula) formed a prominent pair of clumpy, irregular, high surface brightness nebulae (both at least 1/2° across) with NGC 6334 (Cat's Paw Nebula).  The pair is oriented SW-NE, with NGC 6357 on the NE side.  I also viewed this region at 1x handheld using a 7nm H-alpha filter and both nebulae stood out prominently in this fantastic field, which includes IC 4628 (Prawn Nebula) and the Gum 55 loop to its south.

14.5" (8/4/24): NVD at 24x: although NGC 6357 is rather unimpressive visual object, it is a true showpiece with Night Vision and narrowband H-alpha.  The entire filamentary structure forms an open wreath with several outlying spherical and irregular bubbles spanning ~50' or more.  The amount of structure was amazing and could only be partially described by breaking it down into bits and pieces.

#1 is the brightest HII region (known as G353.2+0.9) in NGC 6357 and the main feature seen visually, particularly with an OIII filter.  With a 6nm H-alpha filter, this patch is a very bright, irregular oval E-W, ~3'x1.5'.  The surface brightness is quite high with a small bulge is on the north side. Just south is a very small knot of stars (part of Pismis 24) including HJ 4946, a pair of mag 10.4/11.4 stars at 16" (both O3.5-types with the latter an extremely massive binary).

#2 is a small, fairly bright patch elongated ~N-S, ~3' diameter. A couple of 12th mag stars are involved an may have enhanced the appearance. Located ~9' N of #1 and identified as G353.160+1.042

#9 is an elongated patch, ~6'x3', which is adjacent to both #1 & #2 and roughly centered 6' WSW of #1.  The surface brightness is a little lower than #2 and fairly even except on the south end, which is poorly defined.

#3 is the brightest part of a very long wing on the southwest side. It extends ~10'x2' E-W.  With a careful look, this wing dims significantly but continues to sweep around on the west side towards the north for an additional 15'! (labeled as #12).

#4 is a large, very broad wing on the NE side nearly 20' in length.  It appears dusty with striations but has a much lower surface brightness than #3.

#5 is a bright, circular bubble, ~7' diameter.  The center is darker giving an annular appearance with hole extending towards the W edge!  A mag 6.8 star (HD 157515) is just off the W side. This region is identified as H II 353.09+0.63 (17 25 34 -34 25.2) and is powered by an embedded cluster AH03 J1725-34.4.

#6 is an fairly bright, elongated ~E-W patch, ~5' diameter.  It is situated just ~9' NE of #5.  The south side is brighter and has a sharp border.  The north end is fainter and very irregular. It merges into a brighter triangular patch #7, which is slightly curving (circular arc) on the NW facing side.  Together, #6 and #7 form a partial 7' bubble identified as H II 353.24+0.60, which is described as a "very irregular and patchy morphology".

#8 is a large irregular piece to the E of #1.  It extends ~15' from NW to SE andi s roughly triangular in shape.  The surface brightness is quite uneven or filamentary and the region appears riddled with patchy dust.  Just N of the NE end is wing #4, the largest single feature.

#13 is a fairly large oval , mostly void of nebulosity in the central region to the S of #1. It extends ~10' from E to W.  A strip of nebulosity (not numbered) defines the SE edge and a mag 7.1 star (HD 157258) is just off the E side.

 #11 is a fairly large, spherical bubble in the outskirts on the east side, ~6' diameter. It is identified as H II 353.42+0.45, a classical photo-ionised H II region.  It is located 24' NE of #5 (a brighter annular bubble), at the end of a chain #5 -6-10-11 from SW to NE.  Position: 17 27 17 -34 13.9.

#10 is a small roundish patch, ~2' diameter.  It's near the midpoint of #11, which is ~7' ENE, and #6, which is 7' SW.
