#14 is an outlying fairly faint bubble 38' SE of #1, well beyond the other bubbles on the SE side.  Identified as HII 353.08+0.28 and probably a stellar wind-shaped bubble H II region. 

The designations given are used in the 2016 paper by Russeil et al: "NGC 6334 and NGC 6357: H-alpha kinematics and the nature of the HII regions"

visualUpdates.Name: Sh 2-13
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
NVD at 3x (6/10/26): Using a 3nm H-alpha filter and a monopod, Sh 2-13 appeared as an easily visible circular glow (~40' diameter), attached to the NW side of Sh 2-12.  It was also viewed handheld at 1x with a 7nm H-alpha filter, though appeared more subtle with this combination. The pair forms a Snowman configuration with Sh 2-13 forming the head..

14.5" (8/4/24): NVD at 24x: large, easily visible irregular HII cloud surrounding mag 7.0 HD 158186 (O9.5V binary) and mag 7.6 HD 158103, separated by 11' from SE to NW, with mag 7.7 HD 158020 just off the NW side.  These three stars are nearly collinear and equally spaced. The main section of the cloud is longer in the N-S direction and it's brightest along a thick E-W strip at the northern end which is flattened E-W (gently curved).  A slightly fainter section, with several involved stars, bulges out from the northern part towards the east. It tapers to an apex, making a triangular shape. The opposite western edge is well defined, probably due to dust further west. Overall, the surface brightness is irregular with a strong suggestion of dark patches and or lanes.

18" (6/12/10): At 73x and UHC filter, Sh 2-13 was visible as a very large, irregular glow.  I didn't see the full 40'-50' outline on Megastar, but a roughly 30'x18' glow was visible, extending SW-NE.  On the south side of the glow is a fairly well defined edge, just south of a 15' string of brighter stars oriented SW-NE.  The northern border is also well defined with a linear border oriented SW-NE.  The Milky Way is noticeably patchy in this area and the nebulosity could not be confirmed without a filter, but Sh 2-13 was visible in the 80mm finder at 25x with a UHC filter.

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 6369
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
14.5" (8/8/26): at 316x; bright, fairly small, round, ~30" diameter, annular. Brighter along with rim from the NW to NE side with a bright spot at the N tip. The central hole is relatively large.

24" (7/14/18): at 500x; gorgeous annular planetary with a prominent 30" ring and a relatively large, dark central hole. The rim is noticeably brighter along an arc running from the west side counterclockwise to the northeast.  The rim's surface brightness is quite irregular with at least a couple of sharp brighter spots, the brightest on the northwest rim.

18" (7/14/07): striking view of this annular planetary at 280x.  The 30" halo is punctured by a relatively large 18" hole.  The rim is noticeably uneven in surface brightness with a brighter arc along the northern side.  Spectacular at 700x and the brighter northern rim has a couple of very small brighter spots.

18" (7/22/06): beautiful view at 435x.  The 30" annular ring is brightest along a "C" shaped section from NE moving clockwise to the SW and locally brighter at the NW end.  The central hole is round, well-defined and relatively large compared to the rim.

17.5" (6/30/00): at 500x this planetary has a beautiful annular appearance with a 25-30" halo perforated by a 12" dark hole.  The northern rim is noticeably brighter with a nearly stellar spot near its center.  Located 31' NW of mag 4.8 51 Ophiuchi.

17.5" (6/5/99): bright, beautiful annular planetary at 380x with a well-defined dark central hole.  The rim is clearly brighter along the north edge and slightly weaker on the following edge.

17.5" (7/4/86): bright, fairly small, about 30" diameter, green-blue color.  Appears as a perfect annular ring at 286x with a 15" central "hole".  No central star visible.

13.1" (8/5/83): use at least 220x to clearly resolve the annularity.

13.1" (7/16/82): beautiful ring at 214x and UHC filter, small, slightly elongated.  Visible with direct vision as annular.  The north edge of the rim appears brighter at 312x.

visualUpdates.Name: Nu Dra
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
15x50mm IS binoculars (6/19/09): very easy split in IS binoculars.

10x30mm IS binoculars: beautiful matched pair of mag 5 stars in both the handheld 10x30's and 15x50's.

10x50mm binoculars (8/83): this 62" evenly matched pair of mag 5 stars was easily resolved in binoculars.  This is the faintest star in the head of Draco.

visualUpdates.Name: Sh 2-12
visualUpdates.Visual Description: NVD at 3x (6/10/26): Using a 3nm H-alpha filter and a monopod, Sh 2-12 appeared as a very large, prominent circular glow about 2 1/2° NE of NGC 6357 ("War and Peace Nebula").  It was also viewed handheld at 1x with a 7nm H-alpha filter and was surprisingly obvious. Sh 2-13, a smaller bubble, is nearly attached to the NW side, so the pair forms a Snowman configuration.

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 6397
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
18" (7/8/02 - Magellan Observatory, Australia): The view of this showpiece globular at 171x was amazing at nearly 70° elevation.  It extended across 2/3 of the field - perhaps 20' in diameter.  The cluster was very highly resolved into hundreds of stars, many surprisingly bright at mag 10-11 and overall noticeably brighter than most globulars (1st in ranking of brightest stars).  The globular appeared fully resolved in the halo and even the blazing core was covered wall-to-wall with stars.  Many of the stars are arranged in small groups, chains, curves, etc.  The concentrated core appeared ~3.5' diameter and at 228x had a 3-dimensional appearance with the mag 10.5-11.5 stars layered over a dense, uneven background carpet of stars.  Visible naked-eye.

20" (7/8/02 - Magellan Observatory, Australia): I also had a fantastic view in the 20" f/5 at 212x - the stars seemed to radiate out from the core in spiral curves and completely filled the 23' field!

8" (7/13/91 - Southern Baja): very bright, very large, 10' diameter, irregularly round.  At least 50 stars mag 10-12 are resolved at 63x.  Bright intense core 3' diameter with dozens of stars superimposed and at the edges of the core.  The cluster contains a large halo with many faint and brighter stars superimposed over a mottled background.  Beautiful globular although observed at only 13° elevation from Baja.  This is the nearest globular and first in ranking by brightest stars.

10x30mm binoculars (8/8/04 - Haleakala Crater): picked up very easily while sweeping in IS binoculars close to the SSW horizon from Haleakala.

Naked-eye (8/8/04 - Haleakala Crater): once the position was pinpointed in binoculars, this mag 5.8 globular was just visible naked-eye less than 1 degree NNE of mag 5.3 Pi Arae.

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 6445
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
14.5" (8/8/26): I took a quick look at 226x and 316x as I mainly wanted to admire the wider field containing the globular NGC 6440, which lies 22' SSW.The overall shape is roughly rectangular, with the longer axis oriented NW-SE. The NW side (angling ~SW-NE) is brighter and slightly bowed out in the center. It appears to have a brighter spot just east of center. The interior is slightly darker.

24" (8/14/15): this highly structured planetary as observed using 500x.  NGC 6445 has an unusual rectangular shape, elongated 3:2 NW-SE, with dimensions ~45"x30".  The planetary is brighter in fairly narrow strips along the four sides, creating an annular appearance.  The short NW facing side is slightly brighter and contains a bright knot or section near the middle.  In addition, a faint knot is at the N vertex.  Another bright knot is at the E vertex and either a faint knot or very faint star is at the S vertex.  The short SE facing side is sharply defined and quite straight. A very low surface brightness glow can be seen outside (east) of the eastern vertex.  In addition, with careful viewing an extremely faint outer shell or loop is outside the long SW facing side, connected at the two vertices along this side.  A mag ~15.5 star is just outside the midpoint of the loop.  The outer shell or loop on the NE side was not seen.

18" (7/22/06): this fascinating planetary was viewed at 435x.  The overall shape is rectangular with the longer sides oriented NW to SE.  Both ends are noticeably brighter giving an annular appearance.  The NW end is slightly brighter and irregular in surface brightness with a brighter spot or two.  The rim at the NW end is slightly bowed out and has a well-defined boundary edge in the interior.  The rim at the SE end of the planetary is unusually straight and well-defined.  With averted vision it appeared to extend slightly beyond the main body of the planetary.  The bright lobe at this end is bar-shaped and extended SW to NE in the direction of the minor axis. 

17.5" (7/14/99): this bright PN is striking at 280x with a great deal of structure evident.  It has a boxy appearance, elongated NW-SE with dimensions ~45"x30".  The ends of the major axis are clearly brighter with a bright, shallow arc or crescent-shaped curve on the NW end.  This lobe has an irregular surface brightness with a couple of brighter spots.  The SE lobe is brighter but has an oddly flat edge.  At 380x, the eastern end of the southeast lobe is brighter and has a small extension or nodule that bulges out beyond the rectangular outline to the east.  The center is clearly darker and with careful viewing appears as a dark band running SW-NE.  A mag 12.5 star lies ~45" NW of center and the planetary precedes wide uneven mag 8/10.5 pair (HJ 2810) by 5'.  The planetary forms an unusual pair with GC NGC 6440 20' SSW.

13.1" (8/5/83 and 6/30/84): bright, fairly small, elongated NW-SE, brighter along the NW side.  A darker center visible at 288x appears to cut through the minor axis. The NW edge is slightly curved while the other sides and corners are "boxy" giving an irregular rectangular outline.  The ends of the minor axis are fainter.  A wide double star HJ 2810 = 7.7/10.5 at 41" lies 5.3' E.  A mag 12 star is just off the NW end about 40" from the center.  Forms a striking pair with globular cluster NGC 6440 20' SSW in the same low power field.

13.1" (7/16/82): dark center at 280x appears to bisect the planetary ~E-W.

8" (6/5/81): fairly bright, elongated, uniform.  Located within string of four mag 11/12 stars.

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 6503
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
14.5" (8/8/26): at 226x; bright, large, nearly edge-on 7:2 NW-SE, about 4' in length.  Fairly high surface brightness with a slightly bright core, but no nucleus. The surface brightness is noticeably uneven with a patchy appearance.  Mag 8.6 HD 163465 is 4' W.

17.5" (6/11/88): very bright, large, very elongated 3:1 NW-SE, large brighter core.  The surface has a mottled appearance.  A mag 13.5 star lies 2.2' NNE of center.  Located 3.9' W of mag 9 SAO 8937. 

8" (6/5/81): moderately bright, very elongated, high surface brightness.  A mag 9 star is 4' E.

visualUpdates.Name: UGC 11082
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
24" (8/11/26): at 327x; moderately bright, fairly small, round, 0.6' diameter, very small bright nucleus.  Forms a close pair with UGC 11080 1.9' SW. Situated in a rich field midway between mag 9.1 HD 335505 12' NW and mag 8.5 HD 335506 13' SE.

24" (8/19/25): at 327x; moderately bright, compact, high surface brightness, 30" diameter. Situated in a rich star field within a group of stars

visualUpdates.Name: Webb's Wreath
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
24" (7/14/26): I took a look at Webb's Wreath to pick up CGCG 141-44, which is nearby to the east.  Webb described a semi-circle, including a 7th mag golden star.  The larger 11'x7' oval asterism was striking at 125x.  The two 10th and 11th mag stars at the S end point to CGCG 141-44, an easily visible galaxy.

18" (9/6/10): at 105x, this asterism is fairly striking at low power and consists of 22 stars in an 11'x7' oval ring elongated SSW-NNE.  A half-dozen faint stars lie in the interior of the wreath along with a bright, orange mag 7 star (HD 164922) just inside the wreath on the E side.  On the W side is SLE 90, a mag 11/12.5 pair at 13" with a wide third companion.

Webb's true wreath is probably a smaller asterism consisting of a well defined semi-circle (or semi-oval) of 11th magnitude stars open to the W with the mag 7 star on the S end. The stars are not related in terms of proper motions or distances.

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 6514
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
18" (8/12/10): the emission component of M20 was sketched and observed carefully at 175x.  At the intersection of the dark lanes is the multiple central star H N 40 with a mag 7.6/10.4 pair at 6" and a tight mag 8.7/10.5 pair at 2.3", with the two pairs are separated by 11".  The brighest and ionizing star (HD 164492A) is a massive O7.5-type.

Four lanes (B85) emanate from the bright central hub.  A narrow lane starts NW of the multiple star and heads 2.5' due N, where it stops at a mag 10 star.  Near the base of this lane another branch heads west to the edge of the nebula.  Another lane heads SSE for ~2.5', tapering at the end.  A prominent lane shoots 3.5' NE and has a few short branches, including one just NE of the central stars.  This lane is bordered by a couple of mag 10.5-11 stars on its south edge.  There is an extension at the NE end that bends to the north and exits the main nebulosity and merges with a dusty region just SE the reflection component to the north.  A mag 9.4 star is at the north edge of the main emission component.  The blue reflection component surrounds mag 7.3 HD 164514 and extends ~6' with an irregular structure.

13.1" (4/24/82 and 7/16/82): bright, fairly large, contains three inky black dark lanes (B85) with sharp edges.  Structure is visible along the dark lanes and in the center.  The prominent central star is a quadruple (4th star difficult) consisting of a mag 7.6/10.4 pair at 6" and a mag 8.7/10.5 pair at 2.3", the brighter stars separated by 11".  The NW lane is wider and fainter than the other two lanes but easily traced.  A round, bluish reflection nebula is separated, but very close north.  The view improves using a UHC filter.

8" (many dates from 7/3/80 to 7/16/82): the famous rift structure (3 parts) is fairly prominent with a triple star at the center.  The NW rift is more subdued.  An easily visible reflection nebula is close north.

15x50mm IS binoculars: visible as a small, faint glow surrounding a the central "star".

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 6522
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
24" (8/11/26): at 476x; bright, fairly large, ~3' diameter, very bright core. A few obvious stars are resolved in the halo on the W side. Several very faint stars sparkle on and off in the core region - resolved but not steadily. Otherwise, the core is very mottled or lively.

17.5" (7/11/99): this globular is the larger and brighter of a fairly faint pair with NGC 6528 in the same field just 16' E.  At 220x the halo extended ~2' diameter and contained a very small bright core.  A mag 12.5-13 star is embedded in the NE side.  At 280x, the ~25" core appeared offset east of center and the halo was slightly elongated E-W.  An unresolved string or bar of stars oriented WNW-ENE (just slightly fainter than the core) appeared to pass through the core .  The globular was lively but without distinct resolution.  With averted vision the outer haze increased in size to ~3'.

13.1" (6/29/84): moderately bright, mottled.  A single brighter 13th mag star is on the ENE side.  This is the larger and brighter of a pair of globulars with NGC 6528 15' E in Baade's Window.

visualUpdates.Name: S 698
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
14.5" (7/25/26): wide, bright pair of mag 7.2/8.5 stars at the center of M21 using 66x.

18" (8/12/10): In the center of M21 is the brightest member; mag 7.2 HD 164863.  This star forms a 30" pair (S 698) with mag 8.7 HD 313693. A third bright star, mag 8.8 HD 164883 lies 1.2' NE of the brightest star and extending in a short line NE are two additional mag 10 and 11 stars.

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 6528
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
17.5" (7/11/99): this is the smaller and fainter of an unusual double pair of globulars with NGC 6522 just 16' W.  At 220x, it appears round, ~1.5' in diameter.  The brightness gradually increased towards the center but there was no distinct core.  The surface brightness was fairly smooth overall and the outer halo was fairly well defined.  A mag 13.5 field star is at the SW edge.  The surrounding field was noticeably more vacant than around NGC 6522.  Both clusters can be placed at the edges of the 14' field of the 7mm Pentax XL.  Situated within "Baade's Window" (absorption hole in the Milky Way).

24" (8/11/26): Dark nebula Barnard 298 is just off the SE side and is pretty obvious as a darker and starless patch ~4' diameter that is bordered by three stars around the N end. The surrounding Milky Way is noticeably glowing.

13.1" (6/29/84): fairly faint, small, 2' diameter, not resolved.  This is a smaller and fainter version of globular cluster NGC 6522 15' W.

8" (6/19/82): fairly faint, small, easily visible but no resolution.

visualUpdates.Name: IC 1276
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
24" (7/10/26): at 229x and 375x; large, diffuse glow ~3' diameter. There is no core, but the globular appears patchy. Only a half-dozen or so stars resolve with careful viewing. The cluster is centered just 3.2' SSW of a mag 10.6 star.

24" (9/7/13): at 200x appeared as a fairly faint to moderately bright, roundish glow, ~3' diameter, with a weak concentration.  Grows in size with averted vision to at least 3.5' diameter.  At 375x, a total of 8-10 stars were resolved and a couple more occasionally popped.  The brightest is a mag 13-13.5 star on the west side and a mag 14 star 35" to its east.  A few additional stars appear to be ~15-15.5 magnitude with the remainder closer to 16th magnitude.  A mag 10.6 star is 3' NNE of center.

18" (6/22/09): at 225x appeared as a faint, moderately large, roundish glow with no central concentration.  A string of three stars are superimposed on the north side of the cluster.

17.5" (8/2/97): at 220x, this globular appears as an obvious irregular glow of ~3' diameter with a mag 13.5 star at the west edge.  A superimposed mag 14 star follows [by 36"] and a third mag 14.5 on a line is at the east end.  A mag 15 star was also glimpsed along this string close following the mag 14 star. Appears elongated ~E-W and the irregular outline increases in size with averted vision to 4'x3'.  This faint globular has an unusual mottled patchy appearance although the observed stars may be field stars.

17.5" (7/27/95): at 220x appears faint, moderately large, 3' irregular scraggly outline.  No resolution although the surface brightness is irregular.  A mag 13 star is at the west end, closely followed by a mag 14.5 star.  A similar faint star is situated at the east end.  Located 3' SSW of a mag 11 star.

17.5" (7/4/86): at 105x appears as a faint glow with no central condensation.  Two stars mag 13-14 are on the west side.  At 286x the cluster seems to extend mostly east of the following of the two stars.  Located 3' SSW of a mag 11 star.

8" (7/10/26): at 109x; at my visual threshold and only seen as an ill-defined dim patch about 3' NNE of a mag 10.6 star.

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 6567
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
24" (6/26/25): at 263x, NGC 6567 was easily picked up in a rich star field (the SW end of M24, the Small Sagittarius Star Cloud) packed with mag 10 and fainter stars. It appeared as a fuzzy, small blue disc forming a pair with a mag 13 star 10" W. The star/PN pair is cataloged as ARA 735.  Excellent view at 508x with the disc slightly elongated NNW-SSE.

14.5" (7/17/23): NGC 6567 is situated in a spectacular field at 87x -- remarkably rich in stars with a very obvious dark lane (~25'x6') running ~SW-NE, just west of the planetary.  The correct "star" was highly suspected before blinking because of its slightly soft appearance.  It brightened significantly using an OIII filter. A very small blue disc was clearly resolved at 158x, forming a "double" with a fainter field star just 10" E.  Excellent view at 395x with a crisp edge to the disc and the nearby star well resolved. The PN seemed slightly elongated and irregular at 566x.

18" (8/14/07): picked up at 94x as a "bloated" blue star of 11th magnitude.  Easy to verify with a UHC blink though only a moderate contrast gain.  Situated in a beautiful star field on the SW side of the Small Sagittarius Star Cloud.  A very long dark lane (part of Barnard 304) crosses the low power field from SW to NE, passing to the N of the PN.  In the 80mm finder at 25x, this lane extends NE and is attached to the prominent dark cloud B92 on its SW side.  At 260x, this high surface brightness planetary displays a 10" disc with a 13th magnitude star barely off the east edge.

17.5" (7/8/94): bright very compact planetary at 220x with a mag 13 star at the east edge.  Excellent contrast gain with OIII filter.  At 280x, a high surface brightness small disc was visible and cleanly resolved from the following star.  Has a brighter center but no central star was seen.  Located in a very rich Milky Way field on the SW side of the Small Sagittarius Star Cloud (M24).

8" (8/15/82): appears as a mag 11 "star" at 100x.  Slightly non-stellar at 200x.  A slightly elongated disc N-S is visible at 400x.  Forms a close pair with a mag 12 star just east.  Situated in a rich star field.

visualUpdates.Name: IC 4715
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
8" (7/3/80): IC 4715 refers to the remarkable Small Sagittarius Star Cloud (prominent naked eye object).  Best view at very low power as it extends beyond the edges of the field.  The rich open cluster NGC 6603 is embedded in the NE side.

11x80mm:this is the huge "Small Sagittarius starcloud" and appears as a detached portion of the Milky Way which is a bright naked-eye object in dark skies.  Excellent in binoculars and a magnificent region to scan a low power in all scopes.  Contains true open cluster NGC 6603 at NE edge and dark nebula B92 at NW edge.  This is perhaps the richest large region to scan near the Milky Way rift.

visualUpdates.Name: Sh 2-55
visualUpdates.Visual Description: 24" (8/10/26): NVD at 34x; faint to fairly faint, but obvious elongated patch of nebulosity. Extends in a roughly rectangular shape oriented WSW-ENE, ~4' x 2.5'.  Situated just S and E of a 28" pair of mag 10.3/11.0 stars, wrapping around the south side of the double.

visualUpdates.Name: STF 2342
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
14.5" (7/25/26): unbalanced 34" pair at 122x with a bright mag 6.8 primary and a 10th mag companion due N.. The mag 12.5 secondary was strongly suspected, even with a bright moon and not knowing the orientation.

14.5" (6/30/23): wide and unbalanced 34" pair at 66x with a bright mag 6.5 primary and a large delta V = 3.2. The A component has a mag 12.5 secondary (B) at 14", I didn't notice it.  A mag 8.5 star is 4.5' W and the low power field contains a number of brighter stars.  HJ 864 (6.8/11.0 at 20") is 13' ENE.

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 6705
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
14.5" (8/8/26): at 132x and 226x; M11 is one of the most stunning clusters due to its high resolution, extreme density, and fascinating structure. A 6' N-S string of stars is near the W edge of the main mass of stars. Just to its east is a dense, parallel stream of mostly fainter stars, several with very similar mags and  separations. Along the east edge of the main cluster (separated by a small gap) is another 4.5' N-S stream of up to a dozen stars. Finally, there seems to be a couple of parallel strings of mostly E-W stars on the N end of the cluster.  Right in the center is small, extremely dense ball of resolved stars (~30" diameter) that is bounded by a few small starless patches.

13.1" (many dates from 7/16/82 to 5/27/84): at 140x, several hundred stars mag 11-15 and a brighter mag 8 star (HD 174512) in a 10' region form a remarkably rich cluster including some dense knots of stars.  A starless vacuity is visible just west of center at medium power.  Dark lanes appear to wind through the cluster at high power grouping the stars into chains.  Several dark nebula are near including B108, B112, B318. 

8" (7/16/82): this is the most impressive open cluster with this aperture.  Appears as an extremely rich carpet of faint stars and dense clumps in an arrowhead shape.

visualUpdates.Name: K 4-8
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
24" (7/10/26): at 327x; stellar PN just 4.7'WNW from IC 1295 in field. It is the middle star is a short arc of 5 stars mag 13.1 (on NE end) to 14.3 and appears ~mag 14.2 unfiltered (similar to the 3 middle stars in the arc). Using a NPB filter, the star increases significantly in contrast and becomes the most obvious object in the arc. 

24" (8/12/15): easily visible unfiltered as a mag 14.5 "star", the middle of 5 stars in a shallow 51" arc, concave to the SE. Excellent contrast gain adding a UHC filter at 220x, so it was very easy to identify. Situated just 4.7' WNW of IC 1295, an excellent, fairly large planetary and 19' ESE of globular cluster NGC 6712.

18" (7/22/06): easily blinked at 160x using a UHC filter.  Without a filter appears as a mag 14.5 "star" within a shallow arc of 4 stars located just 5' WNW of the beautiful planetary IC 1295.  The planetary is furthest north of the 4 stars in the short arc and responds well to blinking. Both planetaries as well as globular NGC 6712 are visible in the same low power field of view.

17.5" (7/22/00): this stellar planetary is situated just 5' WNW of IC 1295!  At 140x, visible as a mag 14.5 "star" in the middle of a shallow arc of 4 stars, concave to the north with a slightly brighter star at the east edge.  Excellent contrast gain with OIII blinking and K4-8 appears to "turn on" and becomes brighter than the star on the east end.

17.5" (5/10/86): at 105x and 220x appears as a stellar planetary, estimate V = 13.5-14.0.  Responds well to OIII and Daystar 300 filter.  Located just 4.6' WNW of planetary IC 1295 and 22' SE of globular cluster NGC 6712!  Situated within a close arc of four similar faint stars.

13.1" (7/12/86): verified with UHC blink at 214x.  Appears as third "star" in a close arc of four or five stars, estimate V = 14.0.

visualUpdates.Name: IC 1295
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
8" (7/14/26): at 107x; faint, but fairly easy round glow unfiltered in a rich star field, and brightens nicely adding an OIII filter. Still visible using 5" of aperture.

24" (8/12/15): At 220x + UHC filter, the rim is clearly brighter, particularly along the south side.  But the west side of the planetary is weaker with a darker indentation, creating a "C" appearance, open to the west. A very faint, fairly thin outer shell is visible with careful viewing.  This envelope is roughly the thickness of the brighter rim.  Increasing to 375x and removing the filter, I can count 8 or 9 superimposed stars including several around or just off the edge. The stellar planetary K 4-8 lies just 4.7' NW in the same high power field and NGC 6712 is 24' WNW in the same low power field.

K4-8 was easily visible unfiltered as a mag 14.5 "star", the middle of 5 stars in a shallow 51" arc, concave (opening) to the SE. Excellent contrast gain adding a UHC filter at 220x, so it was very easy to identify.

33" (9/15/07): at 200x appeared weakly annular with a slightly darker hole in the center and slightly brighter rim except on the west edge where there was an indentation or darker notch taking a small bite out of the rim.

18" (7/22/06): at 220x and UHC filter this fairly bright, large planetary was crisp-edged, slightly elongated ~E-W, ~1.5x1.3' in size.  The rim appeared slightly brighter, particularly along the south side giving a weak impression of annularity.  Several stars bracket the planetary and four or five mag 14-15.5 stars appear within the disc at 325x without a filter.  I viewed this object along with NGC 6712 and the stellar planetary K 4-8 in the same low power field of view!

17.5" (6/30/00): fairly bright at 220x using a UHC filter as a roundish disc, ~1.6'x1.4'.  The surface brightness is irregular and it appears slightly brighter along the southwest and northwest portion of the rim.  The unfiltered view at 280x also reveals a mottled appearance with a mag 13.5-14 star situated right at the west edge and a mag 14.5 star in the interior (a bit offset from center).  A couple of extremely faint stars are at the following edge. Located 24' ESE of NGC 6712.

17.5" (5/10/86): bright, large, round, 1.5' diameter.  Very pretty at 220x, estimate V = 12.0-12.5.  The stellar planetary K 4-8 is just 4.6' WNW.

13.1" (7/27/84): the rim on the south or SW side appears brighter but no definite annularity was seen.

13.1" (8/15/82): fairly faint, appears slightly elongated in an E-W orientation.

8" (6/27/81): faint, round, fairly small.  Located 25' ESE of NGC 6712 in the same low power field.  Observation mentioned in 10/81 S&T for the smallest scope!

5": visible unfiltered and easy using a UHC filter at 79x!

visualUpdates.Name: Theta Ser
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
14.5" (7/20/23): striking, wide 22" pair at 76x with very bright mag 4.6/4.9 white components.

15x50mm IS binoculars (6/19/09): excellent close pair at 22", but cleanly resolved.

18" (7/15/03): wide, bright, similar pair (4.6/5.0) at 115x (would be better at lower power).  Both slightly off-white or pale yellow colors.  This star marks the end of the Serpent's tail and is an easy double for any scope.

10x50mm binoculars (8/83): just resolved in binoculars.

visualUpdates.Name: HJ 5505
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
14.5" (7/25/26): perfectly balanced mag 9.4/9.5 pair at a comfortable 15" using 66x.

14.5" (7/20/23): easy 15" pair at 66x with identical mag 9.4/9.5 stars.  The northeastern of the pair is yellow or orange-yellow.

visualUpdates.Name: V Aql
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
24" (10/1/16): gorgeous deep red carbon star admired at 124x and 200x.

18" (8/26/06): remarkable copper-red color at 115x.  Shares the same low power field with pn NGC 6751.

18" (9/3/05): superb example of a deep red carbon star.  At 115x, a very deep orange/red color (B-V = 4.2) is striking in a rich Milky Way field.  Period = 353 days.  The planetary NGC 6751 is located 30' SE.

8" (8/15/82): beautiful deep red color.  Three mag 7-8 stars, roughly in a line, are just west of the filed.  Located 40' E of mag 4 12 Aquilae.

15x50mm IS binoculars: though probably too faint to be seen naked-eye, V Aql is readily visible in the 50mm IS binoculars as a fairly faint, red star.  Located 40' E of a mag 4 star and just over 3 degrees east of M11 and the Scutum star cloud.

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 6755
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
24" (8/27/14): although the listed diameter is 15', the most eye-catching region extends only 5' and is described as the southern group in the earlier observation.  The stars are arranged in two main groups.  On the west side is a "U" shaped group of a dozen stars, open to the northwest, with the brightest mag 10.3 star at the SW end of the loop.  A nice unequal pair (~12" separation) is ~40" SE.  Another couple of pairs (one very close) is along the E side of the loop.  A smaller (~2' dia) but richer group of a dozen stars is 2'-3' NE.  A long looping string of ~20 stars, including two 10th magnitude, begins close SE of this group and curves to the S and W, ending in a small knot of 4 stars. The region between this loop and the two groups described above contains 10-12 mag 15 stars.

17.5" (8/8/91): at 140x this is a bright group of 80 stars mag 10-14 in a 10' diameter.  The stars are arranged in two groups separated by a fairly wide, obvious dark rift oriented SW-NE.  The southern star group is larger and richer (about 50 stars) and contains several stars in two rich subgroups.  The northern group is also catalogued as Czernik 39. A mag 10 star is at the west edge of the northern group.  NGC 6756 lies 30' NE.

8" (8/28/81): large, scattered, two parts are resolved into rich clumps.

visualUpdates.Name: STT 371
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
14.5" (8/1/26): excellent, fairly well balanced mag 7.0/7.5 pair (delta seems less than 0.5) at a tight 0.9". The seeing is good and the pair is split cleanly and steadily at 395x. A mag 9.8 star (C) is at 47".

14.5" (9/23/24): this fairly well matched 0.9" pair was elongated even at 158x. Increasing to 264x, the pair was just resolved with a wide mag 9.8 C component to the west by 47". At 395x, the split was wider but the seeing didn't really support this power.

24" (5/25/14): very close pair, clearly resolved at 500x.

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 6792
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
24" (8/11/26): at 327x; fairly bright, large, elongated 5:2 SW-NE, relatively large bright core. A mag 10.6 star is just 1.5' NW.

24" (9/29/24): at 202x; fairly bright and large, elongated 2:1 SW-NE, ~1.3'x0.6'. Contains a bright, elongated core. The surface brightness is irregular or mottled. Situated in a rich star field with a mag 10.6 star 1.5' NW.

14.5" (8/11/23): at 158x and 226x; fairly faint, elongated 2:1 SW-NE, 1.0'x0.5', brighter core.  A mag 10.6 star is 1.5' NW.

UGC 11430, located 12' NNE, appeared very faint, fairly small, round, diffuse, low even surface brightness, 25"-30" diameter.  A mag 13.4 star is just off the NE edge.

13.1" (7/20/85): fairly faint, prominent bright core, faint extensions SW-NE.  Located 1.5' SE of a mag 10 star.  Forms a pair with UGC 11430 12' NNE.

visualUpdates.Name: Sh 2-79
visualUpdates.Visual Description: 24" (8/10/26): NVD at 34x; only the SW portion of this large region of nebulosity was seen. It appeared as a moderately large, low contrast patch, widest at the N end and tapering towards the S.  The best defined edge is along the E side, which is oriented NE to SW. This section of Sh 2-79 is situated immediately south of mag 9.1 HD 231241, which is the southernmost star in a curving chain of 9th and 10th mag stars.

visualUpdates.Name: Cr 399
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
15x50mm IS binoculars (6/19/09): easy, large naked-eye glow with a few of the brighter mag 5 stars resolved.  Excellent in 15x50 binoculars which frames the asterism beautifully.

18" (8/14/04): the Coathanger asterism (not a true cluster) is an easy naked-eye patch west of Sagitta.  Striking in 10x30 IS binoculars where the triangular coathanger outline is very evident with the long side to the north.  Too scattered and large to look good even with the 31 Nager at 73x (67' field).  There are 10 mag 5-6 stars which dominate the view and another dozen stars mag 9.5-11 scattered throughout the field with no dense areas.  Contains a wide, unequal pair ∑2521 (6/10 at 27") with an orange primary.

16x80mm finder (date unknown): about two dozen scattered stars are resolved in the "Coathanger" asterism.  Includes three mag 5 stars and six mag 6 stars.  This is an easy naked eye group and is striking in binoculars.  NGC 6802 lies due east.

visualUpdates.Name: Terzan 8
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
24" (7/14/26): Night-vision (unfiltered) at 126x; four mag 15-15.7 stars are resolved (three obvious) in the small core (~0.6'), and an additional four stars from mag 14.5-15.7 in the halo. The background glow of the cluster was difficult to see due to the general bright background unfiltered.

24" (8/27/14): picked up fairly easily at 260x as a faint or fairly faint, moderately large, round glow.  A quasi-stellar nucleus stands out or perhaps a brighter superimposed star.  At 375x, a mag 15-15.5 star is cleanly resolved on the east side of a very small core (less than 30").  Occasionally 1 or 2 fainter nearby stars in the core flicker in and out of view.  The overall size was difficult to estimate, but perhaps extended 1.5'-2'.

17.5" (6/30/00): at 220x appeared very faint, round glow, just 1.2' diameter.  The surface brightness is irregular with a couple of extremely faint stars involved.

17.5" (7/20/98): at 220x initially appeared to have a small bright core surrounded by a very low surface brightness halo 1.5'-2' diameter (boundary difficult to trace) within a rich Milky Way field.  With concentrated viewing, I noticed a couple of close mag 15 stars just SE of center contributed to the impression of a small bright core and the background glow was otherwise unconcentrated.  The cluster is surrounded by several mag 13 and fainter stars.  More difficult to view than Terzan 7 also observed on same evening.

Terzan 8, along with Terzan 7 and Arp 2 may be gravitationally bound to the Sagittarius Dwarf Spheroidal galaxy (Sgr dSph).

visualUpdates.Name: [Hubble25] V
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
24" (7/14/26): at 327x; fairly bright H II knot in Barnard's Galaxy (unfiltered) about 0.4' diameter. Forms the NW vertex of a triangle with a mag 12.4 star 1' SE and a mag 13.6 star 1' SSE.  Thought of as an arrowhead, the mag 12.4 vertex stars points to fainter IC 1308  3' E..

48" (5/16/12): bright, fairly small, irregularly round.  This irregular HII region spans 20"-25" and has a higher surface brightness than IC 1308 3' E.  A bright knot is it the SE end.

18" (7/12/10): picked up unfiltered at 175x, though there is a contrast gain with a UHC filter at this magnification.  Best view was unfiltered at 225x and 285x.  This HII knot has a higher surface brightness than IC 1308 and may be slightly smaller at 20".  Located 1' NW of a mag 12.5 star.  IC 1308 is 3' due E.

18" (8/30/08): picked up unfiltered at 175x as a small, 20"-25" knot that was visible continuously.  Mild contrast gain using a NPB filter.  Located 1' NW of a mag 12.5 star.  This HII knot is the slightly brighter of a pair with IC 1308 3' E at the north end of Barnard's Galaxy.

17.5" (9/1/02): at 140x-280x (unfiltered) this is preceding of an 3' E-W pair of fairly easily visible HII regions at the north end of Barnard's Galaxy.  There is a good contrast improvement using an OIII filter at 140x.  This knot is slightly smaller of the two but has a higher surface brightness.

17.5" (7/14/99): at 220x and 280x (unfiltered) this is preceding of a pair of easily visible HII regions at the north end of Barnard's Galaxy.  There is a mild contrast improvement using a UHC filter.  A very challenging HII region, Hubble III, lies 4.4' WNW.

17.5" (8/21/98): easily picked up unfiltered at 220x on the north edge of Barnard's Galaxy as a 25" round knot forming the preceding of a pair of HII knots along with IC 1308. Did not compare view with OIII filter.

17.5" (5/10/91): this object is an HII region on the north edge of NGC 6822.  At 82x and OIII filter, appeared as a very small faint knot, round, approximately mag 14.  A mag 12 star lies 2' SE.  Not seen unfiltered.  Forms a pair with similar IC 1308 = Hubble X located 3' E.  Discovered by Frank Leavenworth in 1887 but Dreyer failed to enter it into the IC as he may have assumed the observation referred to Barnard's galaxy itself.

8" off-axis mask (7/28/19): at 174x; very faint and small but definite with averted vision (no filter).  Can hold for several seconds but not continuously.  IC 1308 was at my threshold and only glimpsed a couple of times.

visualUpdates.Name: IC 1308
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
24" (7/14/26): at 327x; moderately bright H II knot, ~25" diameter/ Appears a bit fainter than Hubble 5, just 3' W. A mag 12.5 (brighter of a double) is 1.6' SE.

48" (5/16/12): bright, fairly small, irregularly round.  At ~30", this HII knot is slightly larger than Hubble V and more uniform in surface brightness but the brighter portions of Hubble V have a higher surface brightness.  This is the easternmost of four HII knots along the northern side of Barnard's Galaxy.

18" (7/12/10): easily visible unfiltered at 225x and stands out fairly well at 285x as a 25" knot (irregularly round). Situated 1.7' NW of a mag 12/14 double star at ~8" separation.  This is the slightly fainter of a similar pair of HII knots at the north end of NGC 6822 with Hubble V just 3' W.

17.5" (9/1/02): the eastern of two HII regions at the north end of Barnard's galaxy. Easily visible with averted vision at 220x without a filter and there is mild contrast gain using an OIII filter at 140x.

17.5" (7/14/99): following of a pair of HII regions with Hubble V at the north end of NGC 6822 = Barnard's Galaxy. Visible with direct vision at 220x and 280x without a filter. There was a mild contrast gain using a UHC filter at these magnifications.

17.5" (8/21/98): easily visible at 220x without a filter as a 30" round knot along with Hubble V just 3.1' W. Because I had no problem viewing this HII region without filtration I didn't blink or use an OIII filter.

17.5" (5/10/91): HII region on the NE edge of NGC 6822. At 82x and OIII filter, appeared as a faint, very small but clearly nebulous round knot. Estimate mag 14. A mag 12 star lies 2' SE (very close double on the POSS). Not seen without a filter. Forms a pair with similar Hubble V just 3' W.

visualUpdates.Name: Sh 2-77
visualUpdates.Visual Description: 24" (8/10/26): NVD at 34x; not seen with 6nm H-alpha filter.

visualUpdates.Name: Sh 2-90
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
24" (8/10/26): NVD at 34x; in addition to the nebulosity that spreads S and SE of the main thick C-shaped nebula, I noticed a diffuse nebulous ring about 2.5' diameter is immediately E of the southern half of the "C". A mag 12.2 star is at the center. Sh 2-89 is 25' SSE.

24" (7/30/24): NVD at 34x: quite a nice object with H-alpha night-vision. This HII region appeared as a beautifully "etched" thick "C" (with south up) over 4' in diameter and opening to the east.  I described it as etched because the outline has a sharp, high contrast. Low surface brightness haze spreads to the  east on the south side and encompasses a 12th mag star.  Also a very low surface brightness glow is evident just to the S and SE. Sh 2-89 is 25' SSE, though I didn't notice it in the field.

18" (9/25/06): I was surprised to easily pick up this faint emission nebula unfiltered at 115x as I missed it on 7/20/98 from the Sierra Buttes with the 17.5".  It appeared as a large, ~5'x4', diffuse oval glow in a very rich star field.  A number of mag 12-14 stars are superimposed.  There was no response, though, using an OIII or H-beta filter.  The periphery is not well defined but the surface brightness was brighter than the surrounding Milky Way and the observation felt secure despite the lack of filter response.  Located ~18' SW of mag 6.5 HD 187614.

visualUpdates.Name: Sh 2-89
visualUpdates.Visual Description: 24" (8/10/26): NVD at 34x and 71x; Sh 2-89 is a faint or fairly faint 4' patch immediately east of the southern part of a bent N-S string of a half-dozen mag 10.5-12 stars. A brighter mag 9.9 star (SAO 87798) is ~5' E of the nebula. The patch is roughly circular and there appeared to be a brighter spot near the center. But checking an image, this is likely a 13th mag star.  Sh 2-90 is 25' NNW.

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 6838
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
48" (5/17/26): at 375x; M71 resides in a fantastic star field with the stellar density sharply increasing at the nearly linear W edge (oriented SSW-NNE) and the S edge (oriented WNW-ESE) of the cluster. These two "faces" give the custer a wedge shaped appearance (vertex at SW end) with up to 200 stars packed extremely densely in the cluster, rising further in compactness at the center.

24" (9/2/16): at 200x and 375x; beautifully rich cluster mostly defined by an intense triangular central or core region with vertices on the north, southwest and southeast corners and sides ~3', 3' and 2.3'.  Roughly 100 stars are densely packed over the background glow within this triangular outline, though the north end is less well defined.   The surface brightness falls off rapidly outside this core, though the halo includes some brighter stars, and the cluster blends into the fairly rich field density beyond a diameter of 5'.  Open cluster Harvard 20 lies 28' SSW.

17.5" (8/22/87 and 8/5/94): roughly 75 stars resolved in a 5' diameter but with a very irregular ill-defined outline to the halo.  The brightest section is elongated SSW-NNE with dimensions 3'x2'.  The brightest star is on the east side of the core and is a close double.  Located in a rich field with likely many field stars superimposed around the halo.  Located just south of the midpoint between Gamma and Delta Sagittae.

Harvard 20, less than 30' SSW, contains about three dozen stars in a 6'x3' field, elongated ~E-W.  Two bright mag 9 stars are off the west side but the cluster is dominated by 20 mag 12/13 stars.  Also includes a scattering of faint mag 14-15 stars.  A pretty evenly matched mag 12.5/12.5 double star is at the east end and an uneven mag 12/14 double star is to the west of the well matched double.

14.5" (7/27/22): ~50 stars resolved at 264x within a roughly triangular or wedge-shaped outline.

13.1" (7/16/82 and 8/22/87): a few dozen stars are resolved over haze, only weakly concentrated, non-symmetrical shape.  Impression that many faint field stars may be superimposed.  Located in a very rich star field. 

8" (10/4/80 and 7/13/83): roughly 20 faint stars resolved a hazy background with averted.  The west edge is brighter.

15x50mm IS binoculars (6/19/09): bright, obvious glow is elongated with a brighter center.

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 6853
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
18" (8/23/03): breathtaking view at 215x; with the fainter but larger outer lobes increasing the dimensions to nearly 7.5'x6' and the ends of the major axis (southeast and northwest) appear to open up and bulge out further.  With careful viewing, ~10 superimposed stars can be counted including the easy mag 14 central star.

17.5" (6/15/91): very bright, very large, 7'x6', bright dumbbell lobes are oriented SSW-NNE.  The SSW lobe is brighter with a bright outer rim.  Large fainter sweeping side lobes fill in the dumbbell and reverse the major axis to WNW-ESE. The planetary has an irregular surface brightness with a darker center.  At high power 5 or 6 stars are superimposed including the easy mag 13.8 central star.  Overall, this is the most impressive planetary.

13.1" (8/15/82): central star easily visible along with a half dozen faint superimposed stars.

8" (9/25/81): central star faintly visible at 200x. The fainter side lobes are prominent.

15x50mm IS binoculars (multiple dates): easily the most prominent planetary visible in binoculars.

visualUpdates.Name: Sh 2-115
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
24" (8/10/26): NVD at 34x; moderately bright, extremely large irregular nebulosity with structure and details, but no very high surface brightness portions. Still, it is a fairly impressive complex. The brightest part is a 6' or 7' kidney-shaped patch roughly 6' SE of mag 7.7 HD 196331 (and just S of cluster Be 90).

This patch is detached from a long, curving stream of neb'y that begins ~8' N of the eastern end of the kidney-shaped region. It curls to the W, wrapping around the mag 7.7. star and then dipping S to mag 5.8 HD 196178, with a total length of at least 25'!  Slightly fainter neb'y extends further SW and SE of the bright star. In addition, very faint neb'y flows out to the NE from the end where I began this paragraph.

On the N end of the complex is a very large, irregular or streaky nebula trending NE to SW. It involves a number of stars including mag 8.9 SAO 49816 and mag 7.8 HD 196090 on its N side.  PN Abell 71 = Sh 2-116 is just 14' further NW of the latter star.

visualUpdates.Name: 48 Cyg
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
14.5" (7/18/24): Striking at 66x with a subtle but noticeable color difference. The northern primary is bluish-white and the secondary has a warmer pale yellow tint.  Located about 2° NW of 52 Cygni, which is near the center of NGC 6960 (western half of the Veil Nebula).

12x36mm IS binoculars (7/18/24): fairly bright binocular pair with well balanced mag 6.3/6.5 components at 3.1' separation.

visualUpdates.Name: MCG -01-53-012
visualUpdates.Visual Description: 24" (8/27/14): at 280x, appeared very faint, very thin edge-on 5:1 N-S, 1.0'x0.2', low surface brightness with no core but slightly brighter central region.  I could almost hold this superthin continuously with averted once I locked in my sweep spot.  A mag 12.7 star is 2' NE and a mag 13.5/14.5 pair [11" separation] is 0.5' N of the brighter star.  Located 1.4° SSW of HCG 88 (NGC 6976/6977/6978 triplet).

visualUpdates.Name: MCG -01-53-014
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
24" (7/23/20): at 375x; exceedingly faint, very thin ghostly sliver ~E-W, only occasionally glimpsed with concentration, though confirmed.  This difficult galaxy is surrounded by a mag 11.5 star 2.0' WNW, and mag 12.8 star 1.3' S and a mag 12.5 star 1.5' NE.  At the time of the observation (end of the session when tired), HCG 88D was well east of the meridian, so it was not situated in an ideal location in terms of altitude and sky brightness.

24" (9/27/19): at 225x; extremely faint, small, elongated smudge only occasionally popped.  Easily the faintest in the HCG 88 quartet.  Situated 5' SW of NGC 6977 (middle of 3 in line).

18" (8/3/05): HCG 88d was searched for at the end of the night and the best I can say is that it was suspected a couple of times, but I couldn't verify the sighting.  This galaxy is misidentified as NGC 6975 in all modern catalogues.

18" (7/21/04): faintest of quartet in HCG 88.  This edge-on galaxy is located ~5' SW of the trio of NGC 6976, NGC 6977 and NGC 6978.  The observation was marginal: an extremely faint glow was only glimpsed a few times with concentration and averted.  I sketched the elongation in the correct orientation (WSW-ENE), which confirmed the sighting. This galaxy is misidentified as NGC 6975 in MCG, PGC as well as the Deep Sky Field Guide.

visualUpdates.Name: Barnard 352
visualUpdates.Visual Description: 18" (7/30/03): At 73x (31mm + Paracorr), this is a fairly high contrast 10'x8' dark cloud in a rich Milky Way field, slightly elongated ~E-W.  A gently curving line of 4 or 5 stars runs ~N-S through the dark nebula, slightly east of center.  The edges of the cloud are ragged and I had the impression of several small fingers of dark nebulosity jutting out from the main body.  This dark nebula is situated just north of the North America Nebula, ~1.2° NNW of center.

visualUpdates.Name: IC 1369
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
18" (7/30/03): this fairly rich open cluster was picked up while observing dark nebula Barnard 361 located 20' S.  At 73x using a 31mm Nagler, it appeared as a partially resolved glowing spot.  Increasing to 215x, approximately two dozen stars were resolved in a boxy outline, roughly 4' diameter.  The stellar density is lower in the center of the group and the cluster is set over some unresolved haze.  Sh 1-89, a faint planetary, lies 20' E.

13.1" (9/3/83): 15 faint stars over haze, fairly small, appears rich.  

8" (8/12/83, Mt. Hamilton): at 100x; rich glowing spot with many very faint stars at visual threshold over haze with averted.  Also a small group of five stars is in the field to the E.  The wide pair STTA 215 = 6.5/7.5 at 2.3' separation is also in the field 18' WSW.

visualUpdates.Name: IC 1396
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
17.5" (8/22/98): the "Elephant's Trunk" is an unusual cometary globule (associated with star formation) on the west side of IC 1396, a huge but faint HII complex. The highest contrast was using a UHC filter at 100x.  A 15'x5' lane was evident oriented WSW-ENE, particularly by gently rocking the scope back and forth. The "tail" of the globule or elephant's "trunk" heads west and is weakly illuminated on the edges, particularly on the south side.  Near the "head" is a mag 9 star (HD 239710) and a pretty double star (STF 2813 = 9.2/9.6 at 10") to the west is embedded in the lane.  With careful viewing the "trunk" shows variations in width and opacity.  The head is located ~18' W of the triple star STF 2816 (5.8/7.7/7.8 at 12"/20"). The massive O-type primary is the main ionizing source of the nebula.

17.5" (8/12/96): This HII region is most prominent with a UHC filter at 100x surrounding the triple star (HD 206267 = STF 2816 = 5.8/7.7/7.8 at 12" and 20").  The multiple star is at the center of a scattered cluster, although nebulosity was not apparent throughout the entire field.  About 25' W is a pretty double star (STF 2813) whose components are aligned with the triple star.  The surrounding 1° field contains a scattered cluster of brighter stars which are fairly uniformly distributed.

In the 16x80 finder unfiltered, the entire cluster is clearly encased in a faint glow at least two degrees in diameter though the nebulosity seems to be more prominent along the curving lanes of the cluster.  The Daystar 300 filter gives a mild enhancement but dims the stars so the overall view is not as pleasing.  Mu Cephei (Herschel's Garnet Star) is at the northeast edge of the nebulosity, ~1.5° from the center.

18" (7/11/10): Barnard 161 is an easy 6' circular dark patch within IC 1396 (north of center) just 13' N of ∑2819 = 7.4/8.7 at 13" and 25' NE of the triple star STF 2816 = 5.8/7.7/7.8 at 12" and 20".  Stands out fairly well at 73x.  There are extensions to the north of this cometary dark nebula that I didn't see.

16x80mm (9/29/84 and 8/26/89): using a UHC filter appears as a very large, irregular nebulous glow (about 2° diameter).  Very faint but definite when compared without filter.  Surrounds STF 2816 = 5.8/7.7 at 12" and a large, faint, scattered star group.  Visible without a filter as an extremely large, hazy region surrounding STF 2816 and fainter stars.

NVD at 1x with 6nm H-alpha (11/30/21): IC 1396 was a very large, prominent circular glow using a handheld 1x image-intensifier monocular (Gen3 Un-Filmed White Phosphor model) and a narrowband H-alpha filter.  The nebula showed darker structure and subtle lanes.

visualUpdates.Name: BL Lac
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
14.5" (8/8/26): I used an AAVSO chart (with comparison mags) to easily identify the field of BL Lac, which is situated 9.5' SSE of mag 8.4 HD 209438. The blazar is just 24" W of a mag 12.9 star. At 226x, it was clearly visible as a mag ~14.3 star (appearing stellar).

18" (7/31/08): Using a finder chart at 280x I was able to identify a mag 15-16 "star", just 25" W of a mag 13 star.  At moments, BL Lac seemed quasi-stellar, perhaps 2"-3" diameter, although it was a bit too faint to feel confident. 

BL Lac was first discovered in 1929 as a variable "star".  It is the prototype of a category of AGN known as blazars, which are essentially low-luminosity quasars viewed directly down the axis of their powerful jets.

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 7209
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
24" (8/12/26): very nice, low power Milky Way cluster and field. At 125x, at least 125 stars resolve, including numerous 10th and 11th mag stars with some brighter stars around the periphery. The cluster extends roughly 20', but there is no distinct boundary to measure. The most distinctive feature is a winding stream of 10th and 11th mag stars that start at the SE end, extend to the north, and then bend to the W. The stream can be broken into three distinct sections or groups at the SE side, E side and NW side ("Y" shaped in eyepiece).

15x50 IS binoculars (6/19/09): while observing Barnard 168, the fairly prominent, long dark lane that begins near M39 and heads east in the direction of the Cocoon Nebula (IC 5146), I picked up this fairly faint, round, diffuse patch that was easily visible in binoculars.  NGC 7209 is perhaps two degrees further ESE and collinear with the B168 dark lane.

17.5" (10/12/85): 100-125 stars are resolved, bright, large.  Located in a very rich field so does not stand out conspicuously. 

13.1" (9/22/84): about 75 stars, bright, fairly scattered. 

8": fairly large, spread out, similar magnitudes.  Framed by an 8th magnitude star.

visualUpdates.Name: LEDA 214803
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
24" (8/12/26): at 327x; faint, small, diffuse glow but not difficult..

17.5" (8/1/86): very faint, very small, slightly elongated.  Located west of a star just off the N side of NGC 7223.

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 7223
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
8" (8/12/26): at 109x; faint, small, diffuse glow, but not difficult with averted. A faint mag 13.8 star is off the S end.

24" (8/12/26): at 329x; moderately bright, oval 4:3 ~N-S, broad, weak concentration, at most 1' diameter. A mag 13.8 star is just off the SE end.  A mag 15.2 star is 1' NW of center and companion LEDA 214803 is just SW of this star. It was faint and very small, but not difficult at all. Situated in a rich Milky Way field.

17.5" (8/1/86): moderately bright, fairly diffuse, slightly elongated ~N-S.  There are two stars to the south including one at the S edge. Brightest in a group (LGG 453).

Forms a close, physical pair with PGC 214803 1.0' NW.  The companion appeared very faint, very small, slightly elongated.  It's situated west of a star off the N side of NGC 7223.  Also UGC 11927, located 8' WSW, appeared faint, fairly small, elongated SW-NE, very diffuse. 

13.1" (8/17/85): fairly faint, moderately large, diffuse, elongated N-S.  Extends from a star on the south end in a fan-shape.  A faint star is off the north end.  A knot was suspected just west of the star at the north end (probably PGC 214803).

visualUpdates.Name: CGCG 530-014
visualUpdates.Visual Description: 17.5" (8/1/86): very faint, very small, slightly elongated.  Picked up about 8.8' NW of NGC 7223.

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 7243
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
17.5" (10/12/85): at 83x, 150-200 stars are visible in a 20' field.  This is a striking cluster at low power and includes a number of fairly bright stars.  Near the center is the nice pair STF 2890 = 9.4/9.7 at 9".  The cluster is irregularly distributed into subgroups.

13.1" (9/22/84): about 80 stars resolved, rich, fairly large, excellent low power field, includes double star STF 2890.

visualUpdates.Name: IC 1442
visualUpdates.Visual Description: 17.5" (8/5/94): about three dozen stars in a distinctive curving row oriented SW-NE about 4' diameter with fainter loops at both ends.  A mag 9 star SAO 34248 is off the SE and a mag 10 star SAO 34250 is off the NE end.  The cluster is unconcentrated but stands out well at low power (100x).  Located 20' SE of NGC 7245 (misplotted on MegaStar).

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 7248
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
24" (8/12/26): at 327x; between moderately bright and fairly bright, strongly concentrated with a bright core that increases to a very small bright nucleus. Bracketed by two double stars to the E and W. The galaxy forms the E vertex of a nearly equilateral triangle with a mag 10 star 8' W and a mag 10.6 star 7' NW.

24" (9/2/16): at 375x; fairly bright, moderately large, elongated 5:2 NW-SE, 1.25'x0.5'.  Strong concentration with a very bright slightly elongated core that increases to the center.   The outer extensions have a low surface brightness.  Sitated in a rich star field between two doubles; a 12" pair is 2' E and a 8" pair is 2.7' W.  NGC 7250 is 17' ENE.

24" (8/7/13): at 375x appeared fairly bright, elongated 2:1 NW-SE, 0.9'x0.5', sharply concentrated with a bright oval core that increases to the center and a moderately large halo.  A 12" pair of mag 13.5-14 stars lies 2' E, a 7" pair of mag 12-12.5 stars is 2.7' W, and finally a 10" pair of mag 14 stars lies 3' WNW.  Not surprisingly, this galaxy is located in a Milky Way field. NGC 7250 is 17' ENE.

13.1" (8/54/84): fairly faint, small, very elongated 5:2 NW-SE, small bright nucleus.  Two faint double stars are near including a mag 13/14 pair at 12" located 2' E.  NGC 7250 lies 17' ENE.

8" (8/12/26): at 109x; very faint, small patch, no details other than a brighter center.

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 7250: [HMR16] 07
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
24" (8/12/26): at 327x; very small HII knot at the NNW end of NGC 7250. It is situated just off (or beyond) the W edge of N tip.

24" (9/2/16): at 375x; the HII "knot" attached on the west side of north end of the galaxy extends ~20"x10" NNW-SSE (slightly different PA than the main galaxy), increasing the total size of the merged glow to nearly 1.0'x0.3'.  NGC 7248 is 17' WSW.

18" (10/19/06): a very faint knot (PGC 214816) is ocasionally visible at the NNW end.  This nearly stellar "knot" is often noted as an interacting companion, though it's a bright HII complex in the galaxy.

Note: HyperLeda catalogs the knot at the north end as PGC 214816 (galaxy), but the HST image clearly shows a massive HII/star-forming complex.

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 7250
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
24" (8/12/26): at 327x; moderately bright, elongated ~5:2 N-S, sharp concentration with a very small bright core.  A small, faint H II knot is visible on the W side of the N end, and it is not aligned with the major axis of the galaxy.  A mag 10.9 star is just off the S end, aligned with the orientation of the galaxy. NGC 7248 is 17' WSW.

24" (9/2/16): at 200x; this disrupted galaxy or interacting pair appeared moderately bright, elongated 5:2 N-S, 0.7'x0.3', bright core.  A small, very faint knot or extension (HII complex) is at the north end. A mag 10.9 star is 0.9' SE of center.  At 375x; the "knot" attached on the west side of north end of the galaxy extends ~20"x10" NNW-SSE (slightly different PA than the main galaxy), increasing the total size of the merged glow to nearly 1.0'x0.3'.  NGC 7248 is 17' WSW.

24" (8/7/13): moderately bright, fairly small, elongated 5:2 N-S, 0.75'x0.3', sharply concentrated with a very small brighter nucleus.  A mag 11 star is just off the SSE edge.  The structure at the north end was masked by Type-Ia supernova 2013dy at mag 13-13.5, which was discovered on July 10th, a couple of weeks before maximum.  The supernova was 2" W and 25" N of the nucleus of NGC 7250.

18" (10/19/06): fairly faint, fairly small, very elongated NNW-SSE, 0.6'x0.2', very small bright core.  A mag 11 star is just off the SSE end.  The galaxy fades at the tips, so the full extent was difficult to determine but appears to extend to 1.0'x0.25'.  A very faint knot (PGC 214816) is occasionally visible at the NNW end.  This nearly stellar "knot" is often noted as an interacting companion, though it's likely a bright HII complex in the galaxy.  NGC 7250 is classified as a starburst galaxy.

13.1" (8/25/84): fairly faint, very elongated streak NNW-SSE, small bright core.  A mag 11 star is off the SSE tip 0.9' from center.  Pair with NGC 7248 17' WSW.  This galaxy may be an interacting double system but it was not resolved.

HyperLeda catalogues the knot at the north end as a galaxy (PGC 214816), but the HST image clearly shows it's a massive star-forming complex.

8" (8/12/26): at 109x; very faint streak extending NNW of a mag 10.9 star.

visualUpdates.Name: IC 5217
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
8" (9/22/22): IC 5217 is fairly easy to identify at 95x in a very rich star field just 2' N of a 10th mag star and 7' SE of a 7'-long gently curving string of 10-12th mag stars.  A mag 7.4 star is 4' N of the northern tip of this string. It blinks strongly with a NPB filter in comparison to the nearby mag 10 star. At 175x, it appears as a slightly fuzzy pale blue "star" and increasing to 225x and 275x, it is definitely non-stellar.

14.5" (7/27/22): identified at just 66x as a bluish "star" (slightly soft appearance) with an excellent contrast gain blinking with a NPB filter.  An ideal 10th mag comparison star is just 1.8' S -- it's brighter than IC 5217 unfiltered, but fainter filtered.  Definitely appears non-stellar increasing to 122x and 158x.  At 660x, the small planetary is elongated 4:3 or 3:2 ~N-S and 6"-8" in diameter.

24" (8/8/21): immediately noticed at 200x appears as a fairly bright soft blue (non-stellar) glow. Excellent contrast gain with a UHC filter. At 260x, seen as a small, high surface brightness blue disk in a pretty star field.  At 500x, IC 5217 seemed slightly elongated N-S and it was clearly extended ~8"x5" N-S at 750x and 1000x.  The central star was not seen.  A striking chain of ~10 stars mag 10-12 extending 7' SSW-NNE lies ~8' NW.  The brightest star is at the south end of the chain.

18" (7/2/08): picked up easily at 174x as a "soft" mag 11.5 with a pale blue color.  Good contrast gain blinking with an OIII filter.  A brighter mag 10 comparison star lies 1.8' S but blinking with the filter the planetary switches apparent brightness with this star.  At 435x, IC 5217 appeared as a 7"x5" blue disc, slightly elongated SSW-NNE.  With direct vision, a slightly brighter quasi-stellar center was visible suggesting the central star was just below the threshold of visibility.

18" (12/08/07): picked up at 115x as a soft blue-grey "star".  Good contrast gain using a NPB filter.  Without a filter, a brighter mag 10 star lies to the south though with the filter the planetary matches the star.  At 225x a definite small disc was visible, crisp-edged, round, ~6" diameter.  The seeing was too soft to use high power.

13.1" (10/10/86): at 166x appears fairly bright but just non-stellar.  Good contrast gain with OIII filter.  A bright compact bluish disc is visible at 214x, slightly elongated.  Estimate V = 11.5 and 5" diameter.  Located 1.3° due south of mag 4.4 Beta Lac.

8" (11/5/82): stellar planetary at 100x, slightly fuzzy at 220x and an easy ellipse is visible at 400x. Observation from home.

visualUpdates.Name: Sh 2-138
visualUpdates.Visual Description: 24" (7/14/26): NVD at 71x; small, slightly elongated glow NW-SE, ~1' diameter. An 11th-mag star is at the NE edge and mag 8.6 HD 23991 is 2.7' E.  Sh 2-139 lies ~23' SE, adjacent to a mag 7.3 star.  This small classical H II region contains four buried O/B-type stars in a similar arrangement as the Trapezium in M42.

visualUpdates.Name: V375 Lac Nebula
visualUpdates.Visual Description: 24" (8/12/26): at 229x; faint but obvious glow, ~1'-1.5' in diameter, involving the young Herbig A4e star V375 Lac = LkHa 233. This reflection nebula is mostly evident to the west of the star in the general direction of mag 8.5 SAO 52153 (2.8' W of V375 Lac). The SW side is brighter and better defined. A bright, wide double star (HJ 1786 = 7.0/9.6 at 44") is 6.7' NNW.

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 7448
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
24" (8/11/26): at 375x; bright, fairly large, elongated 2:1 ~N-S. Contains a brighter core with an occasional stellar or quasi-stellar nucleus.  The galaxy is slightly brighter on the northern half and a 10" knot (H II complex) is often visible at the NW tip of the halo. A mag 10.2 star is 2.5' E of center.

48" (10/26/16 and 10/28/2019): at 610x; very bright, large, elongated ~2:1 N-S, 2'x1', interesting structure with knots.  The central portion is brighter along the major axis like a weak bar and in the center is a small, very bright nucleus.  A bright, prominent knot, 10"-12" diameter, is just west of the northern tip of the galaxy and a weak knot is close east [by ~15"].  The northern half of the galaxy is generally brighter with a slightly mottled surface.  The galaxy has a weak enhancement along the SW edge of the halo [spiral arm] and a fairly faint knot is on the SE side [40" SE of center].  Overall, the southern part of the halo has a lower, more uniform surface brightness.

17.5" (9/19/87 and 9/14/85): bright, large, elongated 2:1 NNW-SSE, small bright core, fainter extensions.  Brightest in the NGC 7448 group.

13.1" (9/22/84): fairly bright, broad moderate concentration, thin fainter extensions NNW-SSE.  Does not contain a well-defined nucleus. 

8" (9/25/81): faint, small, elongated.  NGC 7454 is located 29' NNE.

visualUpdates.Name: UGC 12423
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
48" (10/22/11): at 488x, this extreme superthin appears as a fairly bright, large, razor-thin edge-on, extending ~10:1 NW-SE, ~2.5'x0.2'. It contains a bright, very thin, elongated core that bulges very slightly.  The extensions fade gradually at the tips.  A string of mag 15 and fainter stars oriented WNW-ESE begins near the southern tip.  UGC 12426, a much fainter superthin, lies 9.6' NNE, and NGC 7518 is 6.5' due south.

24" (1/1/16): this superthin galaxy (axial ratio 10:1) appears as a very faint, very thin streak at least 8:1 NW-SE, ~1.4'x10", with a very small brighter nucleus.  The SE extension is longer than the NW.  Situated directly between a mag 10.8 star 2.3' SW and a mag 12.7 star 1.8' NE.

17.5" (11/1/86): very faint but moderately large, thin edge-on NW-SE, very low surface brightness.  A group of faint stars is close east.  Located 2.3' NE of a mag 10 star and 6.6' N of NGC 7518.

visualUpdates.Name: UGC 12426
visualUpdates.Visual Description: 48" (10/22/11): UGC 12427 is the fainter and smaller of two superthins, along with UGC 12423 situated 9.6' SSW.  At 488x, it appears as a fairly faint, very thin edge-on, stretching 0.8'x0.1' in a N-S orientation.  The surface brightness is fairly low and nearly even with a slightly brighter center.

visualUpdates.Name: Jones 1
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
24" (8/12/26): at 200x and NPB filter; large, fairly unique planetary with two slightly curving arcs, centered on the S end and NNW end, forming the brightest portion of the rim.  They were very faintly connected on the W edge, but disconnected on the E side.  The arcs created a "horseshoe" appearance.

24" (10/2/21): at 87x and OIII: I took a quick look at this very large, impressive annular PN at the end of the night.  Initially it seemed the entire rim was visible, but on closer inspection, the E side was disconnected.  The western rim had a low surface brightness, but was clearly connected., creating a huge irregular "C" shape.  The two bright arcs on the N and S side were well defined and pretty straight, with the northern rim brighter.

18" (11/13/07): large, striking planetary at 115x and OIII filter.  Due to its odd horseshoe or toilet-seat shape, it was difficult to estimate a total size but appeared roughly 4.5' in diameter.  Very evident are two fairly bright, very shallow arcs along the rim - one along the S side and other on the NW side.  The arcs are relatively narrow and pretty flat or straight, with a length of ~2' each.  The northern arc is slightly brighter than its counterpart and is brightest at the west end of the arc and gradually fades out as it starts to bend S at the NE end.  The two arcs barely merge on the W end of the planetary but appear disconnected on the E side creating a huge open horseshoe shape.  The interior is filled in with low surface brightness haze.  Faintly visible unfiltered at 115x though the structure was more difficult to discern. 

18" (11/6/04): faintly visible unfiltered at 115x which also reveals a number of faint stars are peppered across the face of the planetary (several in a string).  Beautiful view of this huge annular planetary at 115x and OIII filter with two, fairly narrow bright arcs along the north and south side and a dark center.  The northern arc has a higher surface brightness, particularly near the NW end.  The two arcs come close to merging on the west side, but the eastern side is disconnected yielding a horseshoe appearance.

17.5" (8/21/98): this object, which is one of my favorites, was striking at the Sierra Buttes. This huge annular planetary (nearly 5' diameter) is dominated by two relatively narrow bright arcs in the rim along the NNW and SSE sides which are faintly attached along the west side. The center is quite dark and appears open on the east side giving an unusual horseshoe or "C" shape.

17.5" (8/10/91): at 100x with OIII filter; moderately bright, very large, about 5' diameter.  This huge annular planetary has a distinctive "C" shape open at the east end with a very dark center.  There are two narrow bright arcs in the rim along the NNW and SSE sides.  The brightest and widest arc is along the NNW end.  The two arcs are faintly connected along the western edge.  Impressive object in dark skies using OIII filter although also dimly seen unfiltered. 

17.5" (11/29/86 and 8/13/88): Impressive huge annulus at 62x using an OIII filter.  Bright knots are prominent at the NNW and SSE ends, dims along the east side.

17.5" (9/14/85): marginal object without a filter, but the OIII filter transforms Jones 1 into a huge annular planetary with two brighter sections to the rim.

13.1" (8/11/85): at 62x with OIII filter; faint, very large, clearly annular.  Contains brighter arcs along the north and south portion of the rim and dimmer along the eastern edge.

visualUpdates.Name: MCG -01-60-012
visualUpdates.Visual Description: 24" (8/12/26): between fairly faint and moderately bright, slightly elongated, 30" diameter, bright core, very small bright nucleus.  Forms a pair with MCG -01-60-011 8.5' NW.

visualUpdates.Name: BU 1223
visualUpdates.Visual Description: 24" (11/13/16): this close (~1.5") large mag contrast pair (delta V = 2.6) was striking with an excellent split at 432x.  The seeing was very steady (dewy conditions).  The double star BAR 19 = 9.2/9.5 at 1.0" is 27' ENE.

visualUpdates.Name: BAR 19
visualUpdates.Visual Description: 24" (8/12/26): beautiful 1.0" pair, very close but resolved cleanly at 327x and widely split increasing to 457x.

visualUpdates.Name: Hoag's Object
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
48" (4/6/13): at 488x, an extremely low surface brightness glow surrounding the easily visible core was fairly confidently seen.  The halo appeared slightly brighter along the north side.

48" (5/15/12): at 375x and 488x, the nucleus was easily visible as a fairly faint, very small, round glow, 15" diameter.  The detached outer ring was at the limit of visibility and visible occasionally as incomplete arcs.

48" (4/4/11): at 375x Hoag's Object was easily visible as a faint, small, round disc, 0.3' diameter.  Every so often the seeing improved and the nucleus appeared as a sharp stellar point within the disc, but the detached outer ring (45" diameter) was not visible in poor seeing.

18" (7/2/08): at 280x Hoag's Object appeared extremely faint, very small, round, 20" diameter, low even surface brightness.  Visible roughly 1/4 to 1/3 of the time with averted vision and could hold only a few seconds at a time.  Only the core was visible with no indication of the extremely faint outer ring.  Situated just east of the midpoint of an 8' line connecting two mag 10 and 11 stars oriented SE to NW.  Several fainter stars are grouped to the south of the mag 11 star.

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 2129
visualUpdates.Visual Description: 17.5" (12/20/95): bright, fairly rich group surrounding two mag 7.5 and 8 stars (HD 250290 and 250289) oriented N-S.  There are about three dozen stars mag 10-14 in a 5' well-detached circular group with several double stars, including a faint pair preceding the northern mag 8 star.  The southern mag 8 star has a couple of very faint companions.

visualUpdates.Name: NGC 2371
visualUpdates.Visual Description:
48" (4/1/11, 3/1/19, and 4/23/25): I was stunned by the view of this bipolar nebula at 610x. There was so much intricate detail in NGC 2371/72 that it barely resembled the previous views through my 17.5" and 18" scopes.  The most prominent feature is a pair of irregularly round, very bright nodules on the SW and NE side of the boxy, elongated central region.  Each nodule was distinctive and varied in surface brightness and shape with the SW lobe brighter.  Filamentary streamers or a "hairy tail" extended from the NE node towards the NW and similar wisps extended mainly SE from the SW node, creating a sense of rotation around the fairly bright mag 14.9 central star. The interior and sides were filled with much fainter nebulosity.  A very faint filament connected the main lobes on the NW edge.

Two amazing outer wings (similar in visibility) were detached from the main 1' structure and symmetrically placed 1' NW and 1' SE from the central star.  These wings or "polar caps" were easily visible without a filter at 488x (though increased in contrast with a NPB filter) and both extended ~40"x10" in a SW-NE orientation, increasing the total diameter to 2'.  A mag 13.5 star lies 1.5' NW (beyond the NW wing) and a mag 16 star is 50" NE of center.

24" (4/13/18): at 220x and NPB filter; the detached NW outer wing (1' from center) was faint but not difficult as an extended strip of nebulosity ~30"x10", oriented SSW-NNE.  A mag 13.8 star is outside the wing to the west [1.5' from center]. The slightly fainter trailing wing required averted vision to glimpse, but appeared symmetrically placed 1' SE of center and well detached from the central bi-polar body.

17.5" (2/14/99): very unusual appearance at 380x with two bright knots oriented SW-NE about 30" between centers and 0.9' in total length.  The SW knot is 15"-20" in size, slightly elongated and the brighter of the two.  The NE condensation has a slightly lower surface brightness and appears ~20" in diameter.  The faint mag 14.9 central star is symmetrically placed between the knots.  Weaker nebulosity connects the two knots giving a "dogbone" appearance with a very faint rounder halo encasing the structure!

17.5" (2/13/88): unusual planetary, bright, moderately large, elongated SW-NE.  Two bright knots are at both ends (with two NGC designations) although the SW end is brighter and more concentrated.

13.1" (2/25/84): two condensations in halo.  The WSW side is brighter and sharper.
